title: Leveraging New Technologies to Combat Food Waste: The Case of the "EcoFeast Connect" Philanthropic Platform
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title: Leveraging New Technologies to Combat Food Waste: The Case of the "EcoFeast Connect" Philanthropic Platform
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the critical global issue of food waste and explores how modern digital technologies can be leveraged for philanthropic purposes. By analyzing "EcoFeast Connect," a conceptualized yet technologically realistic mobile and web application, the study demonstrates how real-time data, geofencing algorithms, and digital tracking can bridge the gap between food donors and Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs). The paper outlines the operational structure, user roles, data management, and automated matching mechanisms that allow surplus food to be safely redirected to vulnerable populations. Ultimately, it highlights the triple bottom-line benefits-environmental, economic, and social-of integrating tech-driven logistics into humanitarian food distribution.

title: Criteria Is All You Need A Decision Architecture for AI Systems

detail.title: Criteria Is All You Need A Decision Architecture for AI Systems
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dual-level decision architecture for artificial intelligence systems. Its central thesis is that better decisions with AI do not depend only on more capable models, greater data availability, or more advanced forms of automation, but on a better specification of the criteria under which AI systems participate in decision-making processes. Criteria are not treated here as a fixed list of objectives or preferences, but as the structure that enables a decision architecture to delimit the relevant context, establish admissible reasons, identify the uncertainty relevant to the decision, assess decision closure, and calibrate system autonomy. The proposed architecture operates at two levels. At the system level, it defines decision domains, context boundaries, admissible criteria structures, closure conditions, autonomy modes, escalation rules, and revision mechanisms. At the instance level, it applies that structure to a concrete case in order to determine whether the system may inform, recommend, act, defer, or escalate. This distinction makes it possible to separate decision architecture from models centered on an individual choice: its main object is not to select the best alternative in the abstract, but to specify the conditions under which AI may participate effectively and responsibly in recurring decision domains. The paper introduces the concept of decision closure as the condition under which the relevant context, the applicable criteria, the uncertainty relevant to the decision, and the normative constraints are sufficiently specified to justify a given mode of AI participation. From this perspective, autonomy should not be maximized, but calibrated according to the degree of closure achieved. The central contribution of the paper is to show that a decision architecture is not a defensive layer added to the system, but a condition for converting computational capacity into effective decision participation.

title: Fiscal Architecture of Displacement: Sovereign Finance and the Recurrent Fiscal Obligation Problem

detail.title: Fiscal Architecture of Displacement: Sovereign Finance and the Recurrent Fiscal Obligation Problem
detail.abstract: Displacement governance is typically framed as a coordination problem, requiring better institutional alignment, or a legal gap, requiring stronger normative frameworks. This paper argues that neither framing adequately captures the primary constraint, which is structural and fiscal in character: sovereign financing systems are organized around bounded liabilities, temporary expenditure, and reversible commitments that are categorically mismatched with the mobile and long-term realities of displacement. The result is what this paper calls the recurrent fiscal obligation problem-the institutional difficulty of converting exceptional displacement expenditure into ordinary sovereign obligation-a constraint that tends to persist regardless of normative progress or coordination effort. Drawing on public finance literature, sovereign risk frameworks, and displacement governance experience in Southeast Asia, the paper examines how the categorical, temporal, and territorial fault lines that characterize displacement governance are reproduced through sovereign budgeting architectures rather than primarily through legal ambiguity or institutional fragmentation. It then identifies a reform opportunity in what might be described as the resilience turn in contemporary public finance: IFI resilience instruments, adaptive social protection frameworks, and sovereign sustainability financing are increasingly pre positioning the institutional infrastructure that displacement-responsive governance requires, yet displacement remains only partially integrated as a sovereign resilience investment category. The paper argues that sustainable inclusion — embedding displacement-related expenditure within ordinary state systems on terms that are fiscally compatible with sovereign financing constraints — requires engaging sovereign fiscal systems directly rather than continuing to operate primarily through parallel humanitarian financing architectures. Practical reform pathways include integrating displacement into sovereign resilience analysis, designing fiscally bounded inclusion mechanisms, and treating Article IV surveillance and Public Expenditure Reviews as entry points for operationalizing displacement as a macrofiscal risk rather than an exceptional humanitarian contingency.

detail.abstract: GuardianSense is a unified LiDAR-driven family safety platform for smart television and connected device ecosystems delivering two resident-protection modules on a shared on-device AI substrate. Module A (Child Safety) detects minor-aged viewers in real time via 3D point cloud body proportion analysis and enforces age-appropriate content restrictions autonomously with on-device LLM parental alerts. title: The Political Economy of Tokenized-Market Enforcement

detail.title: The Political Economy of Tokenized-Market Enforcement
detail.abstract: The planner's optimum is an open, policed market. But the instruments have owners whose incentives diverge. An issuer captures only part of its market's surplus. So it over-gates. The walled garden is a response to liability, not efficiency. Ex-post enforcement crowds private gating out. Whether it crowds out or in depends on the liability regime. Inducing openness requires committing to enforcement. Capacity or reputation sustains that commitment. The issuer also sets its own transparency. Transparency, openness, and enforcement reinforce one another. An opaque, walled configuration then becomes self-confirming. Only credible enforcement dislodges it. Regulation is institution design, not instrument calibration.

title: On Confusion: A Restatement of Trademark's Likelihood-of-Confusion Test

detail.title: On Confusion: A Restatement of Trademark's Likelihood-of-Confusion Test
detail.abstract:
Trademark law’s most litigated question is decided by a test no one can explain. Every circuit recites its own list of eight or ten or thirteen confusion factors, no court has ever said how those factors combine into an outcome, and scholars have spent two decades cataloging the test’s failures.

Two recent empirical studies have changed the picture. Analyzing more than 4,000 decisions before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board and more than 10,000 federal court opinions spanning 1970 to 2025, those studies demonstrate that just two factors, similarity of the marks and competitive proximity of the goods or services, predict the bottom-line confusion finding with accuracy exceeding 93%. The remaining factors function as structured exceptions rather than coequal inputs to an open balancing exercise: narrow, asymmetric overrides that flip the two-factor prediction in fewer than 7% of comparisons.

This Article translates those findings into doctrine. Adopting the format of a Restatement, it sets out black-letter rules, explanatory comments, and case-derived illustrations that reduce the confusion test to a gated framework: a two-factor threshold that generates a rebuttable presumption, followed by a structured defeater analysis drawn from the secondary factors, with stated extensions for reverse confusion and for procedural application at summary judgment, preliminary relief, trial, and appeal.

Courts can adopt the framework without overruling a single precedent; the black letter restates what courts have been doing all along, and the procedural applications that go beyond current practice are labeled as such. The framework governs only how factor findings combine; the law governing how each factor is assessed remains untouched. The result is a test that is clearer, more predictable, and faithful to what courts actually do.

title: Composability as Percolation: Networks and General Equilibrium of Tokenized-Market Regulation

detail.title: Composability as Percolation: Networks and General Equilibrium of Tokenized-Market Regulation
detail.abstract: Composability is a network property. It is the set of protocols a token can compose with. We recast the on-chain economy as the random graph it is. A gate removes a token from the giant component. This happens once permissioning crosses a percolation threshold. Reach then collapses discontinuously. We embed many issuers sharing one network and one ledger. The gate becomes socially futile. It relocates bad actors rather than removing them. It also fragments shared composability. Enforcement on the shared ledger removes them instead. The decentralized equilibrium over-gates and under-enforces. The fix belongs at the shared infrastructure, not the venue.

title: The Architecture of Compliance: Optimal Regulation of Tokenized Securities

detail.title: The Architecture of Compliance: Optimal Regulation of Tokenized Securities
detail.abstract: How should a tokenized security be regulated? The usual question is stringency: how tightly to screen. We argue the deeper question is architecture: where compliance binds. A gate excludes bad actors in advance. But it destroys composability, the source of a token's value. A ledger instead deters misconduct after the fact. On-chain transparency makes this cheap and accurate. It leaves composability intact. In our model the optimal architecture flips with traceability. Opaque assets are gated; transparent ones are policed. Past a threshold, the ledger dominates outright. Gating can also trigger adverse-selection collapse. So optimal regulation is an open, policed market.

title: The Thread Axis Method: A Pen-and-Paper System for Tracking Asynchronous Input Dispatch Across Parallel Human and AI-Agent Processes
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Thread Axis Method: A Pen-and-Paper System for Tracking Asynchronous Input Dispatch Across Parallel Human and AI-Agent Processes
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Thread Axis Method, an analog system for managing cognitive load in work environments where parallel activity has been restructured by artificial intelligence into a pattern of asynchronous input dispatch. Where earlier accounts of multitasking describe a worker dividing attention across simultaneously held tasks, the present account argues that contemporary knowledge work, particularly work involving AI agents, more accurately consists of a worker feeding discrete inputs to multiple independently running processes and then waiting for each process to return output before the next input can be given. A prompt sent to an AI agent, a message sent to a colleague, an order placed with a vendor, and a question posed to a client are functionally identical in this respect: each is an input dispatched into a process that proceeds without the worker's continued attention, and each will eventually require a further input that only the worker can supply. The cognitive burden this creates is not one of holding several tasks in mind at once but of tracking which of several waiting processes currently require an input, and not losing track of any process during the interval before its output returns. The Thread Axis Method addresses this burden directly. It is composed of four integrated components, each addressing a distinct part of the same problem: an unordered task dump for capturing every process the worker is or will be feeding, an Eisenhower-based tag applied at the point of capture for setting dispatch order, a horizontal execution axis on which active processes are tracked as vertical threads until their loop is closed, and a physical tally counter used to recover attention and re-enter the correct thread after a lapse. The four components form a single system; none is presented as a standalone feature. The framework is grounded in cognitive science literature on working memory limitations (Cowan, 2001; Baddeley, 2003), the Zeigarnik effect (Zeigarnik, 1927), dopaminergic reward processing, and attentional drift research in ADHD populations (Barkley, 1997), and is particularly suited to individuals with ADHD and to knowledge workers operating multiple concurrent AI agents or asynchronous communication threads.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary enterprise AI transformation confronts a structural governance paradox: the competitive imperative to maximize deployment velocity, the fiduciary obligation to generate measurable economic return, and the regulatory imperative to maintain responsible governance are simultaneously non-negotiable yet fundamentally resistant to joint optimization under conventional management frameworks. This paper introduces the AIconomics Trilemma, a theoretical and operational framework that formalizes this structural tension as an analogue to the Mundell-Fleming Impossible Trinity in macroeconomics. The AIconomics Trilemma posits that enterprise AI programs operating under conventional sequential management cannot simultaneously optimize transformation velocity, economic return, and regulatory responsibility, and that the failure to recognize this structural constraint produces characteristic, predictable organizational pathologies. Derived from direct practitioner observation across enterprise AI programs in financial services, professional services, and technology sectors, the framework introduces five organizational archetypes — the Accelerator, the Monetizer, the Regulator, the Decelerator, and the Calibrator — which characterize the observable failure modes of Trilemma mismanagement and the single sustainable equilibrium state. 
The paper formalizes the Momentum @ Risk Equation, a five-component diagnostic architecture incorporating the Velocity Vector, Economic Exposure, Governance Gap, Trust Reserve, and Balance Quotient. The AIconomics Value Stack is introduced as a five-layer return disaggregation model addressing three structural failures of traditional ROI analysis — the horizon mismatch, attribution complexity, and capability equity premium — that render conventional investment evaluation inadequate for AI programs. The Balance Zone construct defines the operational envelope within which velocity, return, and responsibility are simultaneously managed above minimum viable thresholds. Empirical grounding is provided through a practitioner multi-case methodology. The paper concludes with four testable propositions and research implications for scholars in organizational theory, information systems strategy, and technology economics.

title: Prioritizing Blockchain Adoption in Global Trade: An Empirical Evaluation Using the Blockchain Documentation Benefit Index (BDBI)

detail.title: Prioritizing Blockchain Adoption in Global Trade: An Empirical Evaluation Using the Blockchain Documentation Benefit Index (BDBI)

detail.abstract: Global trade remains highly vulnerable to documentary fraud, a systemic issue severely exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic and recent geopolitical disruptions. While blockchain technology and smart contracts offer proven solutions for tamper-proof documentation, current literature lacks a systematic method for prioritizing its adoption across diverse global industries. To address this critical gap, this study introduces a novel quantitative framework: the Blockchain Documentation Benefit Index (BDBI). The BDBI evaluates and ranks sectors based on six weighted criteria: Fraud Prevalence, Financial Magnitude of Fraud Loss, Multi-Party Intermediation Complexity, Regulatory Documentation Burden, Traceability Gap, and Blockchain Adoption Readiness. Drawing on a contemporary dataset of real-world fraud cases and blockchain pilot deployments (2016-2023), the BDBI is applied to six major international trade sectors. The analysis reveals that Marine & Shipping (BDBI: 4.40) and Food & Agriculture (BDBI: 4.15) represent the most critical priorities for immediate blockchain integration. By providing a datadriven roadmap, the BDBI framework equips policymakers with a strategic tool to deploy AIbacked blockchain platforms effectively, ultimately mitigating billions in annual global trade fraud.

title: When AI Does the Buying What Changes for B2B Marketing
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: When AI Does the Buying What Changes for B2B Marketing
detail.abstract: Traditional B2B marketing is designed to persuade individuals. However, AI tools are increasingly taking on buyers' tasks: identifying vendors, comparing them, and shortlisting them. Unlike humans, AI does not react to compelling stories or influential brands. Instead, it works from facts it can check. This note argues that when AI handles buying, marketing's focus shifts from persuading people to being clear, accurate, and easy for machines to read and trust. It makes two contributions: it recasts the AI agent as a new gatekeeper within the organizational buying center, and it advances four testable propositions about how B2B marketing must adapt. The approach is conceptual, synthesizing organizational buying theory with emerging work on AI-mediated search.

title: Business Report: BYD Co. - An Evaluation of Global Branding, Marketing, and Operational Dynamics

detail.title: Business Report: BYD Co. - An Evaluation of Global Branding, Marketing, and Operational Dynamics
detail.abstract: This business report evaluates BYD Company's global branding, marketing, and operational dynamics as it expands into the highly competitive European electric vehicle (EV) market. Amid strict environmental regulations and rapid industry growth, optimising dealership performance is vital to bridging the gap between the manufacturer and European consumers. By introducing advanced analytical frameworks such as predictive modelling and Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA), this study outlines how internal operational efficiencies can be mapped alongside regional external market factors to drive dealership success. A strategic comparative analysis against key market competitors, including Tesla, BMW Group, Volkswagen Group, and Mercedes-Benz, reveals that while BYD holds strong technological leadership, it faces clear challenges in international brand recognition and emotional resonance. Finally, this report delivers a data-driven framework to optimise European operations, providing actionable recommendations centred on cross-departmental collaboration, targeted data analytics, immersive experiential marketing, and the strategic alignment of sales tactics with global brand objectives.

detail.abstract: In addition to sexual politics and interrelationship, the medieval vernacular fiction The Plum in the Golden Vase 金瓶梅 establishes a social web by focusing on the exchange of objects. Recalling a historical tradition of male actors cross dressing as female roles in Chinese theatrical performances, I will compare the minor character Shu-t"ung with professional practitioners, and reflect upon Shut"ung"s embodied femininity within the diaclects of the real and the fictional. For Shu-t"ung"s gendered body, I will extend the notion of the object to the objecthood manifested in characters of the novel. In this regard, I read Shu-t"ung as a human object that embodies the dynamics of circulation. How does Shu-t"ung perform his objecthood from his gendered body? To approach this question, I will focus on one scene on cross-dressing in Chapter 35 of the novel, wherein Ying Po-chüeh asks Shu-t"ung to dress up as a female lead to entertain guests with southern songs. Why does Ying Po-chüeh initiate this demand for Shu-t"ung to dress up as a female lead to entertain him? How do female mains react to lending clothes to Shut"ung? How do the lyrics of the song relate to Shu-t"ung per se? The comparison between Shu-t"ung and professionals leads me to reflect upon the degree of the authenticity of his femininity in a coerced performance, and the interrelation between his objecthood and gendered body. As gendered objects and gender constructs further formulate a figurative circulation of femininity, the novel has multi-layer objecthood manifested through Shu-t"ung"s body, his song lyrics, and his forced performance. I argue that Shu-t"ung"s body and his gender eventually serve as a sexually-neutral site for fabricated femininity and gestural performance of cross-dressing.

title: Beliefs from Cues
affiliations: and Harvard University

detail.title: Beliefs from Cues
detail.abstract: Beliefs often depend on contextual cues that influence which states come to mind. Models of associative sampling capturing this idea give a central role to similarity, which is typically unobserved and in principle very high-dimensional. We show theoretically that, despite this potential complexity, the effects of cues depend only on two sufficient statistics—representativeness and resonance—that summarize how similarity distorts beliefs. Further, these statistics are measurable with simple, pairwise similarity judgments, offering a straightforward method of generating and testing quantitative predictions. In a controlled experiment, we deploy this method and show that belief responses to normatively irrelevant cues closely track model predictions. We also show that large language models can approximate human similarity judgments and extend the approach to field settings. Applying the framework to survey data on personal experiences and macroeconomic expectations, we show that similarity-based predictions quantitatively explain much of the heterogeneity in experience effects across a wide range of experiences and expectation domains.

reference: INSEAD Working Paper No. 2026/39/STR
title: Programmable Strategy: When Strategy Becomes Code
affiliations: Cornell University and INSEAD - Strategy

detail.title: Programmable Strategy: When Strategy Becomes Code

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The dominant frameworks for understanding competitive strategy have long assumed that strategic intent is translated into organizational action primarily through human coordination-plans, structures, managerial decisions, and cultural alignment. This assumption no longer holds in full. As artificial intelligence, algorithmic decision-making, and automated workflows become the primary mechanisms of organizational execution, strategy is increasingly enacted not through human interpretation but through the design of systems that act autonomously, continuously, and at scale. This paper introduces the concept of programmable strategy: the deliberate translation of strategic intent into system-level behavior through rules, decision logic, operational constraints, and infrastructure design. Drawing on research in strategic management, organizational theory, cybernetics, and software engineering, we propose a four-layer Programmable Strategy Stack-comprising Intent, Control, Decision Logic, and Infrastructure-as a framework for analyzing how strategy is compiled from abstract goals into executable organizational behavior. We argue that this compilation process transforms the nature of strategy execution, the role of leadership, and the locus of competitive advantage. The paper identifies implications for strategy theory, organizational design, and the governance of autonomous systems, and contributes to a growing literature on the intersection of artificial intelligence and strategic management.

title: Stock as Currency
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and

detail.title: Stock as Currency
detail.abstract: Going public turns illiquid private equity into acquisition currency. Using a filingwindow industry-return instrument on 6,066 S-1 filers, we find IPO completion raises annual acquisition probability by 12 to 13 percentage points; nearly three-quarters of the induced deals are paid at least partly in stock. The new currency disproportionately buys private, direct-competitor firms. Acquisitions paid in stock underperform cash acquisitions by 21 to 28 percentage points over three to five years and delist 50% more often. Insiders sell into the most richly valued listings; institutions end up holding them. At the IPO, misvaluation acquires real consequences for firms and investors.

title: AI Strategy as Business Strategy: Competing in the Intelligence Stack
affiliations: Cornell University and INSEAD - Strategy

detail.title: AI Strategy as Business Strategy: Competing in the Intelligence Stack

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally restructuring the basis of competitive advantage, yet the existing strategic management literature has not fully articulated how firms should position themselves within the emerging architecture of intelligence. Drawing on and extending classical strategy frameworks-including industry analysis (Porter, 1980, 1985), the resource-based view (Barney, 1991), and dynamic capabilities theory (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997)-this paper introduces the AI Intelligence Stack, a five-layer conceptual framework comprising Data, Model, Decision, Routing, and Interface layers. We argue that in the AI era the three canonical strategy questions-where to compete, how to win, and what capabilities to build-must be reinterpreted through an architectural lens of intelligence. Competitive positioning is no longer solely a matter of industry or market selection; it requires deliberate choices about which layers of the intelligence architecture to control, partner, or accept structural dependence upon. Sustained advantage depends on learning across the interconnected layers, while organizational capability reduces to the coherent integration of human judgment and intelligent agents at each layer of the stack. The framework contributes to emerging research at the intersection of AI and strategy (Iansiti & Lakhani, 2020; Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018) by providing a unified architectural model that bridges positioning, learning, and capability-building in AI-enabled firms.

title: Misallocation of China's Manufacturing in Factor Markets: 1998-2016
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) and China Southern Power Grid Co., Ltd. (CSG)

detail.title: Misallocation of China's Manufacturing in Factor Markets: 1998-2016
detail.abstract: Misallocation in factor markets will hinder the aggregate production efficiency and economic growth. We extend Hsieh and Klenow (2009) to give a novel and more accurate measure of misallocation in factor markets in China by excluding not only the impact of product markets, represented by heterogeneous markups, but also unexpected productivity shocks and measurement errors across firms and years. Using the Annual Survey of Industrial Firms (ASIF) and the National Tax Survey Database (NTSD), we calculate and describe the misallocation in both capital and labor markets among Chinese manufacturing firms from 1998 to 2016. The results show that: (i) Misallocation for both capital and labor declines and the decline tends to be more striking for labor. (ii) Compared with our method, the conventional measurement originated from Hsieh and Klenow (2009) overestimates the misallocation in labor market for all industries and capital for most industries. (iii) Additionally, we decompose the misallocation in factor markets from both dynamic and cross-sectional perspectives. Dynamically, the unweighted average misallocation in both markets shows a downward trend. New entrants exhibit particularly severe distortions. From the cross-sectional perspective, misallocation is mainly concentrated within non-state-owned firms and within provinces rather than between-ownership or between provinces.

detail.abstract: On 10 December 2025, Australia became the first nation to enforce a blanket prohibition on social media access for users under 16, under the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024, with civil penalties of up to AUD 49.5 million for systemic failures to prevent underage account creation. This paper argues that the ban is not merely ethically costly but legally fragile. Applying the Harm Blindness Framework to identify stakeholder damage, the Paediatric Sentinel Effect in Algorithmic Harm to explain why children's experiences predict adult harms, and a doctrinal proportionality analysis grounded in South African constitutional law, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and General Comment No. 25, the authors show that the ban fails on its own terms and would fail doctrinal scrutiny in any jurisdiction applying ordinary children's rights, data protection and proportionality tests. The analysis traces how framing children as a single beneficiary class obscures harm to vulnerable subpopulations, including LGBTQ+ youth in unsupportive households and children in abusive homes who depend on digital platforms for identity formation and crisis support; the perverse incentives the ban creates for platforms, parents and young people; and its failure to confront the root cause of online harm, platform design optimised for engagement, while displacing responsibility onto families. It closes with a comparative assessment carrying direct implications for jurisdictions, notably South Africa, weighing analogous legislation.

title: Comparative Analysis of Digital Banking Regulations Between the EU (PSD2) and Southeast Asia

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Digital Banking Regulations Between the EU (PSD2) and Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: This study conducts a comparative legal analysis of digital banking regulations between the European Union and Southeast Asia, focusing on the EU's Payment Services Directive 2 (PSD2) as a mature regulatory benchmark and the diverse regulatory approaches across ASEAN member states. While PSD2 establishes a comprehensive, harmonized framework mandating strong customer authentication, third-party provider access, and robust consumer protection, Southeast Asian jurisdictions exhibit significant regulatory heterogeneity. The analysis examines how countries like Singapore, Malaysia, and the Philippines have advanced fintech-enabling regulations, while others, such as Indonesia, contend with fragmented regulatory landscapes split between multiple authorities. Particular attention is given to contrasting models of third-party provider access-the EU's legislative obligation for banks to provide data access versus Indonesia's "bank-centric" bilateral partnership approach-and their implications for consumer choice and market competition. The study further explores regulatory gaps in data protection enforcement, liability allocation, and technical standardization across the region. Findings reveal that while the EU offers a coherent, principle-based regulatory model balancing innovation and consumer protection, Southeast Asia's fragmented and developmental regulatory terrain presents challenges for harmonization and cross-border financial integration. The study recommends the adoption of hybrid regulatory models that incorporate centralized oversight, standardized application programming interfaces, and adaptive governance mechanisms tailored to the region's diverse political-economic contexts.

detail.title: Evaluating the Long-run Impact of adopting Revised Family Code on Women's Life Outcomes

publicationDetails.detailsText: KDI School of Pub Policy & Management Paper

detail.abstract: Child marriage remains a major barrier to women's socioeconomic development despite sustained efforts by national governments and international development partners to eliminate the practice. In 2000, the Government of Ethiopia revised the 1960 Family Code by raising the minimum legal age of marriage from 15 to 18 years, creating an important exogenous policy intervention. This study evaluates the longrun impact of the Revised Family Code (RFC) on women's life outcomes and examines the effects of child marriage and age at first marriage on women's socioeconomic well-being. The analysis draws on data from the Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and employs a Generalized Difference-inDifferences (DID) approach with multiple groups and time periods, complemented by Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) estimation to address potential endogeneity. The findings reveal that the adoption of the RFC significantly improved women's life outcomes, increasing the wealth index by 2%, participation in paid employment by 2%, and asset ownership by 0.2%, ceteris paribus. Furthermore, each additional year in age at first marriage increased the probability of achieving a higher wealth index by 0.07, participating in paid employment by 0.07, and owning assets by 0.007. detail.abstract: Child marriage remains a major barrier to girls' education and women's empowerment in many developing countries. In 2000, the Government of Ethiopia revised the 1960 Family Code by raising the minimum legal age of marriage from 15 to 18 years. Owing to regional and temporal variations in the adoption of the Revised Family Code (RFC), this study examines its impact on age at first marriage and women's educational attainment, while also estimating the effect of early marriage on women's education. The study uses data from the Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and employs a Generalized Difference-inDifferences (DID) model with multiple groups and time periods, complemented by an Instrumental Variable (IV) estimation approach. The findings indicate that the adoption of the RFC increased women's age at first marriage by 0.16 years and educational attainment by 0.12 years relative to areas that had not yet adopted the reform, ceteris paribus. Furthermore, the IV estimates reveal that each additional year in age at first marriage increases women's educational attainment by 0.65 years. The study concludes that legislative reform can significantly improve educational outcomes by delaying early marriage. It therefore recommends strengthening the implementation and enforcement of the Revised Family Code through enhanced institutional capacity, adequate financial and human resources, and effective monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to eliminate child marriage and promote girls' education across Ethiopia.

detail.title: Prospect-Theoretic Market States and Momentum Vulnerability
detail.abstract: We examine whether the prospect theory value of recent aggregate market returns identifies months in which cross-sectional momentum is vulnerable to loser-side reversals. We construct a market-level Tversky-Kahneman (TK) state variable from market excess returns over the standard momentum formation window. Momentum underperformance is concentrated in the low-TK tail and remains after controlling for prior market return and volatility. The relation is clearest in the payoff from shorting past losers, and low-TK months are not followed by stronger aggregate market returns. An implementable low-TK exclusion rule raises average returns and improves the annualized Sharpe ratio from 0.45 to 0.69 under an expanding-window threshold and up to 0.75 under rolling-window thresholds, while reducing downside risk. TK conditioning also complements volatility-managed momentum, raising its Sharpe ratio from 0.77 to 0.87. The results identify TK as an ex-ante indicator of conditional momentum vulnerability.

detail.abstract:
Background: Moderate-to-severe anaemia remains common among adolescent girls in India, but field haemoglobin testing is often unavailable. We assessed whether routinely collected NFHS variables can prioritise girls for testing and whether algorithmic complexity can overcome the information limits of survey proxies.

Methods: We developed prediction models in NFHS-5 (2019–21; 115,716 girls aged 15–19 years), using 31 states and union territories for training, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh for validation and threshold selection, and Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand as a geographically held-out test set. NFHS-4 (2015–16; 121,730 girls) was used for reduced-predictor cross-survey robustness analysis because some NFHS-5 predictors were unavailable or system-missing in the harmonised NFHS-4 extract. The outcome was altitude-adjusted moderate-to-severe anaemia. Logistic regression, LASSO, LightGBM, and SuperLearner models were evaluated using survey-weighted AUROC, AUPRC, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and prespecified subgroup analyses.

Findings: In the NFHS-5 geographic test set, AUROC converged across model families (0·521–0·524), despite higher internal cross-validation estimates. LightGBM achieved AUROC 0·524, AUPRC 0·136, expected calibration error 0·055, sensitivity 0·586, specificity 0·442, PPV 0·132, and NPV 0·881 at the evaluation threshold. A 12-variable survey score retained similar discrimination in the geographic test set (AUROC 0·521; NPV 0·880). In reduced-predictor NFHS-4 cross-survey analysis, AUROC was 0·545 for LightGBM and 0·550 for the harmonised survey score. Decision-curve analysis showed no positive net benefit at the selected threshold. At a uniform threshold, sensitivity differed substantially by caste group.

Interpretation: Routinely collected NFHS variables appear to define an individual-level information ceiling near AUROC 0·55 for moderate-to-severe anaemia. Survey-only scores should not be used for diagnosis or individual referral. Their principal value is to show why haemoglobin measurement remains necessary and to guide evaluation of programme-level testing strategies under scarcity, pending prospective validation.

title: Memory Rehearsal and Belief Biases

detail.title: Memory Rehearsal and Belief Biases
detail.abstract: We rely on memory to form beliefs, but we also frequently revisit memories in conversation and private reflection. I show experimentally that such rehearsal generates systematic belief biases. Participants are randomized to have conversations about a subset of experiences, either ones that reflect well or poorly on them, which has large effects on which experiences they can recall a week later. Crucially, participants appear naive about these effects: they take what they remember at face value when later incentivized to form accurate beliefs about their experiences. Participants also make rehearsal choices seemingly without regard to their later distortionary effects. Intrinsic preferences for thinking about positive experiences instead drive rehearsal choices and therefore a positivity bias in recall and beliefs. This mechanism provides a new non-strategic channel through which overly optimistic beliefs can arise and generates novel predictions in a range of economic domains.

detail.title: Regulation as a Financial Stabilizer: Environmental Policy Stringency and Corporate Default Risk
detail.abstract: We examine how environmental regulatory stringency affects corporate default risk. Using cross-country and time-series variation in environmental policy stringency, we document a negative relation between policy stringency and corporate default risk. Quasi-natural experiments based on emissions trading systems and carbon tax adoption, together with corroborative evidence from the 2015 Paris Agreement, support a causal interpretation. Mechanism analysis evidence suggests that tighter regulation encourages firm responses that enhance financial resilience, including higher environmental engagement and environmental innovation, more conservative financial policies, and stronger internal environmental governance. Overall, the findings suggest that although stricter regulation may impose near-term compliance costs, it can promote corporate adjustments that improve longer-run financial stability and reduce default risk.

detail.abstract:
Background: The Cox proportional hazards model, the standard tool for oncological survival analysis, assumes a single shared baseline risk across patients. This assumption is often unrealistic, as biological and clinical variation not captured by measured covariates can bias hazard estimates. Frailty models extend the Cox framework with a random effect representing this unobserved heterogeneity. We compared a standard Cox model with a Gamma frailty model to quantify unobserved heterogeneity in survival among curatively treated patients with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC).

Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 586 treatment-naive patients with OCSCC treated with curative intent, primarily by surgery with risk-adapted adjuvant therapy, at Malabar Cancer Centre between 2014 and 2020. Overall and disease-free survival were estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method. Predictors—including age, sex, pathological stage, tobacco/alcohol use, tumour subsite, and adjuvant therapy—were evaluated using univariate and multivariate Cox regression and Gamma frailty models. Model performance was compared using Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), concordance index, and frailty variance (θ).

Findings: Mean age was 58.2±10.7 years; 71.0% were men and 85.5% reported tobacco or alcohol use. One-, three-, and five-year overall survival were 92.7%, 80.0%, and 73.2% respectively. On multivariate analysis, age, pathological tumour stage, pathological nodal stage, and adjuvant therapy remained independent predictors in both models. The frailty term was statistically significant (θ=1.535, p=0.02), and the Gamma frailty model showed higher concordance (0.825 vs 0.721) and lower AIC than the Cox model, with amplified hazard ratios for tumour stage (1.842 vs 1.588), nodal stage (1.400 vs 1.234), and adjuvant therapy (1.704 vs 1.326).

Interpretation: The Gamma frailty model consistently outperformed the conventional Cox model, confirming clinically meaningful unobserved heterogeneity in OCSCC survival. Incorporating frailty terms improves hazard estimation and risk stratification and should be considered in survival modelling for oral cancer.

Objectives: Insomnia is a highly prevalent disorder; however, access to its first-line treatment, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) remains highly limited. We aimed to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of an intelligent digital CBT-I.

Methods: We conducted a prospective, multicenter, open-label, pragmatic randomized controlled trial comparing the clinical and cost-effectiveness of intelligent digital CBT-I-based diagnosis and therapy for insomnia (IDT) with sleep hygiene education (SH). Adult participants with insomnia disorder were recruited from 4 hospitals in China. Eligible participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either IDT or SH. Outcomes were assessed at 6 week and 3 months. The primary endpoint was self-reported insomnia severity at 6 weeks, measured using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all randomized participants. Cost-effectiveness was evaluated from a societal perspective and expressed as incremental cost-effectiveness ratios and incremental net monetary benefit. The trial was prospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07357779).

Results: Between January 20, 2026, and May 10, 2026, 404 participants were randomly assigned to IDT (n = 202) or SH (n = 202). Of these, 246 participants (60.9%) were female and 158 (39.1%) were male; 228 (56.4%) were younger than 45 years, 127 (31.4%) were aged 45-59 years, and 49 (12.1%) were older than 59 years. At 6 weeks, the mean ISI score was 8.41 (SD, 5.63) in the IDT group and 12.97 (SD, 4.95) in the SH group (adjusted mean difference, -4.56; 95% CI, -5.43 to -3.69; P < 0.001; Cohen d, -0.86). The incremental net monetary benefit was ¥1004.19 at a willingness-to-pay threshold of ¥90,000 per quality-adjusted life year gained. No serious adverse events were reported in either group.

Conclusions: The Intelligent digital CBT-I-based diagnosis and therapy effectively alleviates insomnia symptoms and demonstrates superior cost-effectiveness. These findings suggest its potential for implementation as a first-line treatment for insomnia disorder.

title: The AMA Method -Analytical Foundations of Its Failure

detail.title: The AMA Method -Analytical Foundations of Its Failure
detail.abstract:
In 2024, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, implementing the CRR III regulation, withdrew the Advanced Measurement Approach for operational risk (AMA) — a model built on an actuarial foundation — ending its twenty-year history in the banking sector. The official justification was excessive dispersion of model results across institutions, undermining comparability of capital requirements. This article argues that such dispersion was merely a symptom — the deeper problem being a structural inconsistency of the framework, embedded in its assumptions from the outset.

Three structural properties of the AMA framework are derived. Property (1) concerns the domination of distant quantiles of the aggregate loss distribution by a single extreme loss when heavy-tailed severity distributions are applied. Property (2) demonstrates that the AMA model outcome is determined by quantiles of the severity distribution higher by one or more orders of magnitude than the regulatory quantile of 0.999. Property (3) indicates the dependence of the extreme loss value — which determines the model outcome — on the count of minor, negligible operational events. The occurrence of these properties was verified by a numerical Monte Carlo experiment.

The results indicate that the combined effect of the derived properties led to the necessity of estimation at quantiles of the order 0.9999, 0.99999 and higher — levels beyond the capabilities of reliable statistical modeling given data volumes available in banking practice. Also critical was the ambiguity in the definition of rarity, and the transfer of that concept onto the single loss distribution axis — a transfer arising from the joint occurrence of properties (1), (2), and (3). Rarity readings on this axis depended on the quantile positioning of extreme losses, which could itself depend on the count of low-value, negligible losses. The observed dispersion of results across institutions may therefore have been a consequence of these unintended structural inadequacies, rather than the result of modeling errors.

detail.abstract:
Background: The Asia-Pacific region has the fastest metabolic disease transition globally, yet burden analyses remain global or sub-regional, obscuring the country-level heterogeneity that should guide differentiated prevention and treatment-capacity planning. Type 2 diabetes (T2DM), hypertension, obesity, hyperlipidaemia, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) share a common upstream exposure in the region’s nutrition transition. No study has combined country-level epidemiological phenotyping, demographic decomposition, sociodemographic frontier analysis, and projection beyond 2030 for this five-condition cluster. We characterised the burden, structure, and trajectory of these conditions across 54 Asia-Pacific countries and territories to identify where resource allocation is most urgently needed.

Methods: Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 estimates, we analysed disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and mortality for T2DM, hypertension, obesity, hyperlipidaemia, and MASLD in individuals aged 15 years and older across 54 Asia-Pacific countries and territories, 1990–2023. We applied joinpoint regression and age-period-cohort (APC) analysis to characterise temporal trends, hierarchical clustering to stratify countries into epidemiological phenotypes, Das Gupta demographic decomposition to partition absolute burden change into population growth, ageing, and genuine rate change, quantile regression against the Socio-demographic Index (SDI) to identify burden unexplained by development, and Bayesian age-period-cohort (BAPC) models with integrated nested Laplace approximations to project burden to 2050.

Findings: Age-standardised DALY rates diverged: obesity (estimated annual percentage change [EAPC] +0.59%, 95% uncertainty interval [UI] 0.51–0.66) and T2DM (+0.54%, 0.51–0.58) rose while hypertension (−1.18%, −1.23 to −1.12) and hyperlipidaemia (−1.11%, −1.17 to −1.05) declined, and MASLD increased marginally (+0.17%, 0.10–0.24). Nauru recorded the region’s highest hypertension, obesity, and hyperlipidaemia rates, and the Republic of Korea the lowest hypertension and hyperlipidaemia rates. Hierarchical clustering resolved five geographically coherent phenotypes, from an obesity-driven Oceanian small-island cluster to a stabilising East Asian and high-income cluster. Genuine increases in age-specific rates, distinct from population growth and ageing, contributed 38.9% of the obesity DALY rise in South Asia and 37.4% in Southeast Asia; India recorded the region’s fastest obesity EAPC (+4.77%). Oceanian phenotypes carried excess burden above their sociodemographic development level. Absolute burden is projected to rise across all five conditions to 2050, concentrated in adults aged 65 years and older.

Interpretation: The Asia-Pacific metabolic burden is geographically structured, not a single regional narrative, and regional aggregates risk misallocating resources by treating it as uniform. The five phenotypes require differentiated responses: structural food environment reform in Oceania, expanded dietary and physical activity policy in South and Southeast Asia, and sustained investment in the institutional mechanisms underlying the East Asian and Australasian success trajectories. Health systems across all phenotypes must simultaneously sustain preventive investment and expand treatment capacity to absorb the demographically driven burden growth projected through 2050.

detail.abstract: The application of machine learning (ML) to quantitative finance has grown rapidly, yet financial return series have an extremely low signal-to-noise ratio and are non-stationary, exposing predictive pipelines to severe backtest overfitting. We conduct a rigorous, leak-free, cost-aware stress-test of whether ML models trained only on monthly features derived from daily OHLCV price and volume data can produce economically meaningful, net-of-cost portfolio improvements over disciplined baselines, on a universe of 30 large-cap US equities (2010-2025). A wide spectrum of models, namely regularized linear regressors, tree ensembles, and deep networks (MLP, 1D-CNN, LSTM, CNN-LSTM, Transformer), is evaluated under an anchored walk-forward scheme that retrains at each step, with a pre-specified promotion gate (mean out-of-sample Spearman Rank IC ≥ 0.05 on a 2016 hold-out) that admits only the MLP among the deep models. Promoted forecasts enter a Black-Litterman optimizer as Bayesian views, with Marchenko-Pastur covariance cleaning, dollar-neutral constraints, and realistic transaction costs (10 bps). We report a negative result: in the out-of-sample period (2017-2025) the best model (MLP, Sharpe 0.96) only marginally edges a no-ML Black-Litterman "Prior-Only" baseline (Sharpe 0.94) that shares the same covariance cleaning, while incurring more than three times the cumulative transaction cost (15.13% vs. 4.67%). More strikingly, a naive equally weighted 1/30 portfolio attains a Sharpe of 0.93, essentially tying the entire optimized apparatus. Fama-French five-factor alphas of the active linear and tree strategies are statistically insignificant. The risk-adjusted performance of the pipeline is driven by covariance regularization and Bayesian shrinkage, expressed mainly as superior drawdown control, rather than by the predictive content of the models. We release a fully reproducible pipeline as a baseline for future studies.

detail.title: Two Roads Diverge and Converge in the AI Era: Computer-Generated Works as an Exception for Human Authorship?
detail.abstract:
The intersection of copyright law and artificial intelligence (AI) presents numerous unresolved challenges, while the copyrightability of AI-generated content (AIGC) is particularly complex. Jurisdictions have adopted distinct approaches that converge and diverge in addressing this matter. Classic human authorship jurisdictions, such as the United States (US), China, and the European Union (EU), require AIGC to satisfy human authorship and originality requirements to be copyrightable. As a result, their debates focus on the level of original authorial contributions required for AIGC protection. In contrast, jurisdictions following the computer-generated works (CGWs) doctrine, such as the United Kingdom (UK) and Hong Kong (HK), diverge significantly when applying a plain interpretation approach. These jurisdictions treat AIGC as copyrightable subject matter regardless of originality standard, even though they also generally follow the human authorship requirement. The convergences and divergences among these jurisdictions make their comparison particularly valuable to explore. 


To unpack this convergence and divergence, the article first examines relevant scholarly debates and recent legal developments in classic human authorship jurisdictions (represented by the US, China, and the EU) that illustrate how they address the copyrightability of AIGC. It then explores the CGWs doctrine in jurisdictions such as the UK and HK, highlighting how their approaches may differ significantly. In light of these divergences, particularly under a plain interpretation approach, the article argues that the divergent stance adopted by CGWs jurisdictions is doctrinally problematic and lacks theoretical justification. The article proposes a refined doctrinal approach to the CGWs doctrine that aligns more closely with the frameworks in human authorship jurisdictions regarding AIGC protection. While some divergences may persist, this refined approach establishes a more reasonable and justifiable framework, fostering greater convergence between the two systems.


This comparative analysis offers insights on unified pathways forward for jurisdictions navigating AI and copyright. These pathways include developing a more reasonable originality standard for AIGC, exploring limitations on AIGC copyright protection, and acknowledging the diminishing role of copyright law in the AI era. This recognition of the diminishing role underscores the need for alternative solutions beyond the traditional copyright regime to address emerging challenges more directly and efficiently.

Background: The NHS Health Check is a major cardiovascular disease prevention programme, but long-term evidence on its clinical impact and cost-effectiveness is limited. This study assessed associations between attendance, health outcomes, healthcare costs, and cost-effectiveness over ten years.

Methods: A retrospective population-based cohort study was conducted using linked healthcare and cost data covering 2·7 million people, encompassing years 2015 to 2025. Adults aged 40–74 years eligible for an NHS Health Check were included. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and first major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). Secondary outcomes were cardiometabolic risk factor detection and guideline-directed medical therapy initiation and sustainment. Health economic outcomes included quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Hazard ratios were estimated using time-varying Cox models; all analyses were adjusted using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW).

Findings: Among 925,072 eligible adults, 445,446 (48·1%) attended an NHS Health Check. Non-attendees had a higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR 1·31, 95%CI 1·26–1·35) and first MACE (1·09, 1·05–1·14). Over ten years, this corresponded to one fewer premature death per 116 attendees and one fewer first MACE per 751 attendees. Attendance was associated with gains of 0·11 QALYs for mortality (ICER £9,006 per QALY) and 0·03 QALYs for MACE (ICER £36,923 per QALY).

Interpretation: NHS Health Check attendance was associated with lower mortality, MACE, and favourable economic profile. Reducing inequalities in uptake and improving engagement of non-attendees is necessary to maximise population benefit.

title: An Empirical Test of Rank-Dependent Probability Weighting
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: An Empirical Test of Rank-Dependent Probability Weighting
detail.abstract: Cumulative Prospect Theory (Tversky and Kahneman, 1992) modified Original Prospect Theory (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979) so that decision weights depend on the rank of the outcome. Rank dependence rules out violations of first-order stochastic dominance and extends prospect theory to probability distributions with any number of outcomes. This representation also has sharp, testable empirical implications: given well-documented properties of the probability weighting function, decision weights should be larger for the highest-ranked outcome than for intermediate outcomes. We test whether decision weights are indeed rank-dependent using a large sample of binary choices (1,989 participants and 59,517 choices). The 125 gamble pairs were designed to allow semi-parametric estimation of decision weights. Our estimates show strong evidence for rank dependence: decision weights for the highest-valued outcome are significantly larger than those for the middle outcome. Although both models are statistically rejected, our estimated decision weights are considerably closer to Cumulative Prospect Theory than Original Prospect Theory. Moreover, in an out-of-sample prediction exercise, Cumulative Prospect Theory predicts three-outcome choice percentages substantially better than Original Prospect Theory. Our results thus provide a strong empirical basis for the use of Cumulative Prospect Theory in economic applications.

title: Direct from Syndication: Syndication Costs, Liquidity, and Growth of Direct Lending
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate

detail.title: Direct from Syndication: Syndication Costs, Liquidity, and Growth of Direct Lending
detail.abstract: Middle-market corporate borrowing has shifted away from syndicated loans toward bilateral lending funded by private credit funds. One reason for this shift is the demand uncertainty associated with syndicated lending. We argue that demand uncertainty requires underwriters to have access to liquidity and that the amount of liquidity needed depends on the severity of syndication frictions. We measure syndication frictions using the time in syndication and the flex terms used in the syndication process. Using a large sample of syndicated loan and direct-lending transactions we find that syndication frictions predict borrowers switching to direct lending. For arrangers, we argue that liquidity requirements imposed in 2016 increased the costs of underwriting syndicated loans. Consistent with the liquidity-cost channel, we find a significant increase in the sensitivity of underwriting fees and switching propensities to syndication frictions after the introduction of liquidity requirements. In addition, we find banks that were more exposed to liquidity requirements due to the lack of a large stable deposit base, reduced their liquidity intensive lending activity more than banks with more stable funding sources.

title: Renewable generator bidding: The role of market conditions and power purchase agreements
affiliations: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) - School of Economics, Finance and Marketing, Monash University, Griffith University and Griffith University

detail.title: Renewable generator bidding: The role of market conditions and power purchase agreements
detail.abstract: Our paper examines how wholesale market clearing prices and the presence or absence of long-run power purchase agreements (PPAs) impacts on renewable generator bidding strategies and patterns in Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). We establish and analyse typical bidding strategies of renewable generators in South-Australia, the state with the highest penetration of renewable generation in Australia. We use model-based clustering to identify 22 typical behavioural profiles, which we call strategies, based on the bids of 26 generators on a 5-minute basis during 2023. We analyse these 22 strategies as a function of wholesale market clearing prices, as well as our assessment of the presence or absence of power purchase agreements. We find that most of the time - in line with economic expectations - renewable generators bid predominantly negative or close to zero AUD/MWh, the extent of the negative bids depending on their contractual (revenue) structures and market clearing prices. However, periods of sustained or deep negative market clearing prices are associated with a profile containing 100 % of bids close to or at the price ceiling. We recognise this as potential economic curtailment aimed at avoiding dispatch in the absence of no-floor power purchase agreements. These findings have significant consequences for market and system design. Our results show that the structures of contracts designed to reflect long-term public policy support for new investment are likely to influence spot-market pricing outcome. As such, long-term investment policies should consider design frameworks that are integrated with medium-term risk management and short-term operational market timeframes.

title: The Emission Trading System and Industrial Resilience: Performance and Policy Implications
affiliations: University of Milano - Bicocca - Department of Business and Law, University of Milano - Bicocca - Department of Business and Law, Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca - Department of Business Administration, Finance, Management and Law and University of Milan-Bicocca

detail.title: The Emission Trading System and Industrial Resilience: Performance and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: The EU Emissions Trading System operates across hard-to-abate manufacturing sectors characterised by heterogeneous technological, infrastructural and energy-system conditions. We investigate the relationship between verified emissions, free allocation of allowances, benchmark structures and industrial decarbonisation feasibility across sectors and European countries. The empirical analysis combines an assessment of verified emissions and free allocation dynamics, a benchmarking exercise based on a nonparametric quartile-based performance indicator computed at the installation level, and an econometric analysis on sectoral emissions and carbon intensity. The evidence highlights substantial heterogeneity across sectors and installations: observed ETS exposure depends both on firm-level efficiency and on broader structural conditions, including electricity systems, infrastructure availability, energy costs and access to low-carbon energy vectors. Benchmark-based allocation mechanisms may partially incorporate structural territorial advantages into observable ETS performance outcomes. Industrial decarbonisation is less mediated by the carbon price signal alone than by the interactions among technological readiness, infrastructure deployment and the energy production mix. Where commercially scalable transition pathways remain incomplete, progressively tighter carbon constraints risk materialising faster than firms' practical capacity to adjust production systems.

title: Radiofrequency Ablation Versus Standard Surgery for the Treatment of Second and Third Degree Haemorrhoids (ORION Trial): A Multicentre Double Blind Randomised Controlled Trial
