detail.title: Radiofrequency Ablation Versus Standard Surgery for the Treatment of Second and Third Degree Haemorrhoids (ORION Trial): A Multicentre Double Blind Randomised Controlled Trial

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors have nothing to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Coordinated by Sheffield Clinical Trials Research Unit, and approved by the London–Queen Square Research Ethics Committee (21/LO/0762). Eligible participants provided written consent.
declarations.funderStatement: The ORION trial was funded by the UK National Institute of Health Research Technology Assessment Programme (NIHR131861).
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: The trial was registered on Dec 12, 2021 (ISRCTN14474552).

detail.abstract:
Background: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a new treatment for haemorrhoidal disease. Proponents suggest it reduces postoperative pain and maintains low recurrence rates, however evidence for clinical effectiveness and cost remains limited.

Methods: ORION is a pragmatic, multicentre, patient- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group, randomised non-inferiority trial conducted in 17 acute UK National Health Service hospitals ( ISRCTN14474552).  Adults with symptomatic second- or third-degree haemorrhoids who had failed conservative management were randomised to RFA or standard care (SC).  SC comprised procedures recommended by European guidelines (haemorrhoidal artery ligation, haemorrhoidectomy, stapled haemorrhoidopexy), selected according to surgeon preference. Following patient consultation, postoperative pain (superiority) and recurrence (non-inferiority margin<10%) were selected as co-primary outcomes. The primary analyses were modified intention to treat.

Findings: Between 7th January 2022 and 8th January 2024, 383 participants (mean age 48·6 years, 61% male) were randomised. 179 patients underwent RFA, 152 received SC (131 haemorrhoidal artery ligation, 20 haemorrhoidectomy, one stapled haemorrhoidopexy), and 52 received no procedure. At postoperative day 7, the adjusted mean difference in self-reported pain between RFA and SC was 0·17 (95% CI -0·67, 1·01). Twelve-month recurrence was 47% after RFA versus 39% after SC (adjusted absolute difference 7·4%,95% CI -5·3% to 20·1%). Neither superiority for pain nor non-inferiority for recurrence was demonstrated.  Secondary outcomes (adverse events, symptom severity, incontinence, complications) were comparable. RFA reduced healthcare costs because of shorter operating times (adjusted mean difference 9·1 minutes, 95% CI 7·6, 10·7) and lower consumable costs but patients reported more time off work (mean difference 2·61 days, 95% CI 0·33-4·89).  

Interpretation: These findings do not support the routine adoption of RFA on the basis of improved patient-centred outcomes and highlight the importance of evaluating new surgical technologies before widespread implementation.

title: Forecast-Skill Scarcity, Price Floors, and the Value of Weather Information in Solar-Saturated Electricity Markets
affiliations: University of Tokyo - The University of Tokyo and University of Tokyo

detail.title: Forecast-Skill Scarcity, Price Floors, and the Value of Weather Information in Solar-Saturated Electricity Markets
detail.abstract: How does the economic value of weather information in day-ahead price forecasting depend on forecast skill and on photovoltaic (PV) price-floor exposure? We study the Japan Electric Power Exchange, where nine areas share one market design but differ in PV penetration, on a daily-rolling walk-forward (n = 140 folds, September 2024–October 2025) with paired Diebold-Mariano tests and cluster-block bootstrap inference. A bid-close-admissible operational forecast carries large, broad weather value: on a common all-hours sample, exact-issuance JMA-GPV raises mean weather value about 7x over a reproducible lagged-reanalysis proxy and spreads it broadly. The apparent concentration of value in PV-floor regimes is an artefact of forecast-skill scarcity: a low-skill proxy extracts value only where the weather-to-price map is steep (the PV-floor channel), whereas a skilled forecast resolves demand and wind channels too and the concentration washes out. A threshold-crossing value-of-information model formalises this, reproduced by a controlled noise-degradation of the operational forecast. Two predetermined, non-price quantities pin the low-skill channel's location — the engineering PV/peak capacity ratio (Spearman -0.800) and a physical curtailment-to-FLOOR linkage (near-floor prices 19-96x likelier under PV curtailment; rho = +0.833) — with the price-derived FLOOR rate (rho = -0.733) an observable proxy. Operational skill is economically actionable through floor-event prediction (PR-AUC 0.37 to 0.59), cutting a short generator's realised JEPX imbalance exposure by about 177,000 JPY/MW/year — not battery arbitrage, where the marginal weather contribution is about zero. In solar-saturated markets weather's value is thus large, broad, and decision-relevant under operational skill; only its measured concentration is a skill-scarcity artefact.

title: Financial Inclusion, Fintech, and Financial Stability in Sub-Saharan Africa Using Alternative Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial Inclusion, Fintech, and Financial Stability in Sub-Saharan Africa Using Alternative Models
detail.abstract: The study comprehensively investigates the effects of changes primarily driven by relationships among financial inclusion, Fintech, and financial stability in Sub-Saharan Africa. We employ the Driscoll-Kraay Fixed Effects model, the Panel Fixed Effects regression model, and the Dynamic Panel Threshold model on the yearly data, spanning from 1st January 2004 to 31st December 2024. The study underscores the importance of Fintech and financial stability in achieving digital and stable financial inclusion in Sub-Saharan African economies. The results indicate that Fintech has a positive and statistically significant impact on financial inclusion in Sub-Saharan African economies, suggesting that It plays a crucial role by offering accessible, innovative digital financial solutions. Similarly, financial stability is positively influenced by economic development, enhancing financial inclusion, implying that a stable financial system increases public trust in banks and other financial services providers. These outcomes have significant implications, as they highlight how financial inclusion, Fintech, and financial stability are reshaping the financial services sector and contributing to the development and sustainability of the financial system.

title: Bridging the Global Carbon Data Gap: A Systematic Transfer Learning Framework for Estimating Corporate Emissions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Bridging the Global Carbon Data Gap: A Systematic Transfer Learning Framework for Estimating Corporate Emissions
detail.abstract: Accurate corporate carbon emissions data are essential for climate governance and sustainable investment, yet significant gaps persist across global markets. This study proposes a systematic transfer learning framework for corporate carbon emission estimation and benchmarks performance across 53 countries, six emission scopes, and multiple model families. Using firm-level data from Compustat and S&P Trucost, we compare local baselines, zero-shot global models, and transfer learning approaches. Our results reveal three findings. First, transfer learning effectiveness depends on local data availability: it outperforms local baselines in data-scarce markets (R̄² = 0.825 vs. 0.796; p = 0.003), while local models dominate when data are abundant. Second, transfer learning substantially improves upon zero-shot global models (R̄² = 0.822 vs. 0.626; p =1.2610⁻¹⁰), confirming that cross-country knowledge transfer requires local adaptation. Third, gains concentrate in Scope 3 downstream (Δ = +0.063, p = 0.007) and product-use emissions (Δ = +0.070, p = 0.009)—the most economically significant and difficult-to-measure categories. These findings offer a regime-aware decision rule for ESG data providers, regulators, and researchers seeking to close the global corporate carbon data gap.

title: Industrial Chain, Supply Chain and Value Chain in the Energy Industry: Opportunities and Challenges
affiliations: Wuhan Institute of Technology, University of Auckland Business School, China University of Geosciences Wuhan, China University of Geosciences Wuhan and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Industrial Chain, Supply Chain and Value Chain in the Energy Industry: Opportunities and Challenges
detail.abstract: Ongoing geopolitical conflicts, frequent energy trade wars, and related issues significantly undermine the globalization of the energy market. The pressing questions of today’s and tomorrow’s energy transformation revolve around expanding the energy industry’s industry chain, supply chain, and value chain, as well as enhancing the market-oriented distribution of energy through innovative and transformative approaches. Currently, data have emerged as a pivotal force driving economic growth, fueling the energy revolution, and propelling the advancement of digital technologies for the creation of a comprehensive global and regional energy market. This shift introduces fresh governance concepts, theories, methods, and models. The traditional energy system’s dual challenges of high demand and high emissions exacerbate ongoing coal-power conflicts and impede the market-based reform of oil and gas pipelines. With the rapid digitization of the energy sector and the challenges posed by integrating large-scale renewable energy sources, distributed power supply, and microgrids, there is an urgent need to adopt digital strategies to address the “impossible triangle” of ensuring energy security, economic growth, and efficiency. Thus, exploring digital governance within the energy sector’s industry, supply, and value chains is crucial. This exploration aims to enhance the efficiency of market factor allocation within the energy industry amid the digital economy’s swift expansion and address the broader issues of energy market reform and global integration. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.3390/en17061467

title: Dynamics between Energy Intensity and Carbon Emissions: What does the Clustering Effect of Labor and Capital Play?
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Dynamics between Energy Intensity and Carbon Emissions: What does the Clustering Effect of Labor and Capital Play?
detail.abstract: Energy depletion and environmental degradation have emerged as pressing concerns in the era of China's highquality green economic development. We present an integrated framework that incorporate energy consumption intensity, industrial clustering, and carbon emissions into the STIRPAT framework. Our study examines 30 Chinese provinces from 2006 to 2017. Unlike previous analyses, our study measures industrial clustering from two dimensions: labor and capital clustering. Specifically, the benchmark results confirm that a 1% increase in energy consumption intensity will, on average, raise regional carbon emission intensity by 0.03389%. Moderating analysis shows that labor and capital clustering significantly lower carbon emission intensity by reducing energy consumption. These findings have been consolidated after performing a panel vector autoregressive model. Interestingly, the promoting effect of energy consumption intensity on carbon emission intensity tends to be tightened when labor clustering surpasses a threshold. In contrast, the corresponding effects substantially weaken after capital clustering exceeds a threshold. In all, these findings provide new evidence to understand the energy-emission nexus from an industrial clustering perspective. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2024.142223

title: Nonlinear Subsidy Effectiveness, Path Dependence, and Hysteresis in Off-Grid Electricity Systems
affiliations: University of Saskatchewan, University of Saskatchewan, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Saskatchewan

detail.title: Nonlinear Subsidy Effectiveness, Path Dependence, and Hysteresis in Off-Grid Electricity Systems
detail.abstract: AbstractWe examine whether the effectiveness of the Power Cost Equalization (PCE) electricity subsidy program varies with fuel-price conditions in rural Alaska. Using a panel smooth transition regression model with a two-stage residual inclusion approach to address endogeneity and drawing on data from 96 utilities over 2006–2021, we find that the response to PCE is nonlinear and regime-dependent. A 1% increase in the PCE rate raises residential electricity sales by about 0.14% in the low-fuel-price regime but by 0.09% in the high-fuel-price regime. The estimated transition function further indicates that most utilities operate in the high-cost region, where the PCE primarily functions as a revenue-stabilization mechanism. We further show that fuel-price declines do not necessarily restore earlier levels of subsidy responsiveness. The path-dependence results indicate that fuel prices from two years earlier moderate the current PCE effect, while the hysteresis analysis shows that cumulative exposure to high-cost conditions creates persistent changes in subsidy responsiveness. These outcomes have important implications for the design and timing of subsidy reform, particularly regarding the roles of cost ceilings, benchmark rates, and complementary investments in reducing dependence on high-cost diesel generation.

reference: Energy Economics, 132, 107422. DOI:10.1016/j.eneco.2024.107422
title: Appraising the Role of Energy Conservation and Emission Reduction Policy for Eco-Friendly Productivity Improvements: An Entropy-Balancing DID Approach
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Appraising the Role of Energy Conservation and Emission Reduction Policy for Eco-Friendly Productivity Improvements: An Entropy-Balancing DID Approach
detail.abstract: In pursuit of low-carbon and high-quality economic development, the Chinese government has implemented an energy conservation and emission reduction (ECER) policy. It has piloted this policy for three groups of prefecture-level cities since 2011. So far, there is no systematic evidence to demonstrate whether such a strategy can help China achieve a "win-win" situation between energy conservation and environmental protection. To identify the causal effect of the ECER policy on eco-friendly productivity (EFP), we explore variations in the timing of this policy across cities combined with the entropy-balancing method and assemble a balanced panel dataset encompassing China's 283 cities from 2006 to 2017. Empirical findings demonstrate that EFP in the ECER pilot cities had increased by 15.3% on average compared with EFP in non-ECER pilot regions based on the difference-indifferences framework. Notably, the ECER policy generates significant positive spatial spillover effects on surrounding ECER pilot regions. Our channel analysis confirms that the positive effect of the ECER policy is also realized through energy savings, structural effects, and green technological effects. Moreover, the observed effect is significantly heterogeneous regarding geographical locations, resource endowment, whether a city has an old industrial base, and environmental regulation. Finally, several policy implications concerning China's ECER policy and EFP improvement are put forward. The full paper is available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2024.107422

title: Productivity and Living Standards Are Not Everything: Reassessing Krugman's maxim
affiliations: Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu - Deloitte Access Economics

detail.title: Productivity and Living Standards Are Not Everything: Reassessing Krugman's maxim
detail.abstract: Paul Krugman’s well-known claim that, in the long run, productivity is “almost everything” in determining living standards has become a central organising principle in economic policy debates. This paper argues that the maxim is only conditionally valid within a narrow accounting framework and becomes misleading when applied to real-world economies. Three critiques are developed. First, both productivity and living standards are incompletely measured, particularly through the omission of natural resources and non-market sector outputs. Second, productivity is an inadequate proxy for broader social welfare, which includes environmental sustainability, distributional outcomes, and non-market services. Third, the direction of causality is not one-way: living standards, demand conditions, and macroeconomic policy also shape productivity outcomes. The paper further shows that even within a conventional framework, other factors—including labour force participation, population dynamics, and net foreign income—make non-trivial contributions to long-run living standards. The central conclusion is that the apparent dominance of productivity is a feature of restrictive assumptions rather than a general property of economies. A productivity-centric policy framework is therefore incomplete. Policymakers should move beyond a productivity-centric framework toward a broader dashboard of economic and social indicators. Periods of weak productivity growth may reflect not only economic constraints but also socially optimal choices in mature economies.

title: Analyzing Electric Vehicle users' Intention to use Dynamic Wireless Charging Facilities: A study from New Zealand
affiliations: University of Auckland, University of Auckland - Faculty of Engineering and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Analyzing Electric Vehicle users' Intention to use Dynamic Wireless Charging Facilities: A study from New Zealand

publicationDetails.detailsText: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour, 102, 125-141. DOI:10.1016/j.trf.2024.02.014

detail.abstract: Gaining insights into how users perceive dynamic wireless charging (DWC), also known as dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT), technology for electric vehicle charging is crucial for developing effective measures and policies for its successful integration into the transportation network. This research paper presents a study conducted in New Zealand using an online stated preference survey and employing a structural equation modelling approach. The study investigates users' intention and acceptance of DWC technology, considering various latent factors, while incorporating attributes related to technology acceptance and the theory of planned behaviour in the modelling framework. The findings reveal that perceived concern negatively influences users' intention to use DWC facilities, while perceived usefulness in terms of ease of use and convenience, as well as environmental awareness and social norms, positively impact users' intention. These results offer valuable insights for devising strategies to enhance the acceptance of DWC technology in the future. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2024.02.014

title: Does Energy Efficiency Influence House Prices? Evidence from Spain
affiliations: Banco de España and Universidad Carlos III de Madrid

detail.title: Does Energy Efficiency Influence House Prices? Evidence from Spain
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the impact of energy efficiency on housing prices in Spain between 2015 and 2022. We fit a hedonic pricing model on more than one million transactions for which identification relies on within census-tract-quarter-year variation in Energy Performance Certificates, controlling for dwelling, location, and transaction characteristics. The results show that highly efficient homes (A–B) sell for 9.8% more than the least efficient ones (F–G), with the premium generally increasing over time. However, the capitalization of energy efficiency is heterogeneous: it is stronger for detached dwellings and weaker in tighter real estate markets. Climate effects are also non-linear. Higher heating needs increase the price premium with respect to the least efficient homes, except for the most efficient dwellings. On the other hand, lower cooling needs are associated with larger price premiums only for highly efficient dwellings. Overall, the results suggest that the valuation of energy efficiency depends on property characteristics, market conditions and climate, rather than reflecting a uniform cost-savings mechanism.

title: Modelling the Role of Industrial Structure Adjustment on China's Energy Efficiency: Insights from Technology Innovation

detail.title: Modelling the Role of Industrial Structure Adjustment on China's Energy Efficiency: Insights from Technology Innovation
detail.abstract: Due to uncoordinated economic progress, China's regional gap concerning energy efficiency (EE) is noticeable. However, industrial structure adjustments can be reorganized as a promising way to prioritize the green and lowcarbon transition. Aiming to understand how regional EE can be achieved through industrial structure adjustment, this study empirically investigates the role of industrial structure adjustment in increasing interprovincial EE from a technology innovation perspective. Unlike previous studies, the primary analytical framework is anchored on a spatio-temporal domain. Specifically, we observe that industrial structure rationalization and industrial structure adjustment not only directly influence local EE but also indirectly exert a positive effect on EE improvements in adjacent provinces. The same implications are also valid when addressing the EE-ICT nexus. Further mechanism analysis shows that technology innovation positively moderates industrial structure adjustment to EE enhancements, with regional heterogeneity being all-important. We find that the non-linear effect of industrial structure adjustment on EE is conditioned by technology innovation. Increasing R&D input intensity could significantly change the impacts of industrial structure adjustments on EE efficiency. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2024.140861

title: Governing AI Risk in High-Stakes Deal Environments: Who Controls the Evidence Layer?

detail.title: Governing AI Risk in High-Stakes Deal Environments: Who Controls the Evidence Layer?

detail.abstract:
AI regulation is an area of active, rapid legislative change; readers should verify all dated regulatory claims against current legal sources before relying on them.

Agentic and autonomous AI systems are now embedded across the entire M&A lifecycle - from deal sourcing and diligence through valuation, negotiation, closing, and integration execution. In high‑stakes deal environments, where fiduciary duties, valuation accuracy, regulatory scrutiny, and litigation exposure converge, the evidentiary obligations that attach to AI‑assisted decision‑making remain poorly understood.

Under the EU AI Act and equivalent global frameworks, deployers rather than vendors bear accountability for how AI systems operate in their name, and this responsibility cannot be transferred contractually. Parallel obligations arise under long‑standing legal frameworks that predate AI regulation. Courts and tribunals assessing AI‑assisted decisions focus on reconstructability, human oversight, and professional verification duties. Recent cases across Canada, England, and the US confirm that organisations relying on AI output must evidence what the system did, how human decision‑makers engaged with it, and whether oversight met professional standards.

This paper argues that control of the orchestration layer determines what evidence can be produced across all phases of M&A, and thereby determines deployer liability when AI‑assisted decisions are challenged. Vendor indemnities, representation and warranty insurance, and contractual disclaimers do not address deployer liability under Article 26 or its global equivalents. Drawing on comparative regulatory analysis, cross‑framework mapping, and a working proof‑of‑concept prototype, the paper proposes a layered governance architecture for agentic AI across the full M&A lifecycle, aligned with the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It introduces a model-diverse defensive architecture designed to mitigate adversarial prompt risks through independent validation loops, and demonstrates how architectural choice dictates an organisation’s capacity to satisfy non-delegable evidentiary obligations when AI‑assisted deal decisions are contested.

title: Algorithmic Echelons: The Organization as a Reflection of Its Top Decision Systems
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: Algorithmic Echelons: The Organization as a Reflection of Its Top Decision Systems
detail.abstract: Upper echelons theory holds that organizational outcomes reflect the cognitions, values, and experiences of top managers. Yet algorithmic systems increasingly shape what executives see, how they interpret it, and which alternatives they consider. The strategic apex of the firm is no longer purely human. I reconceptualize the upper echelon as an algorithmic echelon: a hybrid decision-making structure in which human executives and algorithmic systems jointly produce strategic cognition, choice, and outcomes. I identify four mechanisms through which algorithmic systems reconfigure upper echelons theory's central constructs—cognitive substitution, attentional mediation, interpretive opacity, and delegation re-architecture—and derive four propositions specifying when algorithmic echelons amplify, distort, or substitute for the strategic cognition of human top managers. This paper reformulates upper echelons theory's scope conditions for an era of algorithmic organizing and introduces hybrid strategic cognition as a focal construct for strategic leadership research.

title: Above-the-Loop Governance: A Statistical Architecture for Verifying and Allocating Decision Authority in Deployed AI Systems

detail.title: Above-the-Loop Governance: A Statistical Architecture for Verifying and Allocating Decision Authority in Deployed AI Systems

The evaluation framework set out in Sections 2 and 10 is offered as a neutral instrument applicable to every provider claiming the category, and the author holds that any system he builds should be tested against it as rigorously as any other. Readers should weigh the argument of this paper on its merits and against the published framework. detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly make consequential decisions at a volume and velocity beyond human review and increasingly hold authority over those decisions rather than offering recommendations a human weighs. The dominant oversight model, the placement of a human in the decision flow, was designed for a different scale and is now constrained by documented cognitive limitations and by an economic structure whose cost grows linearly with deployment. This paper defines above-the-loop governance: a class of architecture in which qualified human professional judgement is not embedded in the per-decision flow but is held as a continuously measured benchmark against which an AI system's judgements are verified, using statistical methods established over more than half a century in clinical research, regulated manufacturing, and population-grade measurement. The architecture's defining economic property is that the human benchmark scales with statistical sufficiency rather than with AI volume, so the unit cost of governance falls as deployment grows under stable conditions. The paper extends the architecture in three respects: it anchors the human benchmark to externally established professional and regulatory standards, addressing the circularity of an organisation measuring itself; it introduces an authority layer that allocates decision authority between human and machine on measured evidence rather than by default; and it specifies the graded, accountable, measurement-verified response that must follow when divergence is detected. The paper situates the architecture explicitly within the scalable oversight literature of AI safety research and the post-deployment monitoring literature of regulated industries, states the assumptions and limits of each claim, offers a ten-criterion framework by which any system claiming the category should be evaluated.

title: From Mining to Meaning: How Do Blockchain Infrastructure Platforms Respond to Environmental Sustainability Concerns?
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Hong Kong University of Science and Technology - Department of Accounting, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: From Mining to Meaning: How Do Blockchain Infrastructure Platforms Respond to Environmental Sustainability Concerns?
detail.abstract: Environmental sustainability is a critical concern in IT infrastructure governance, yet its implications for blockchain infrastructure platforms (BIPs), such as Bitcoin, remain insufficiently understood. We first provide evidence that Tesla’s 2021 suspension of Bitcoin payments due to its negative environmental impact increased investor awareness of BIPs’ environmental impacts. Consistent with nonpecuniary preference theory in behavioral finance, we find that BIPs, especially energy-intensive proof-of-work-based platforms, experience losses in token valuations following the suspension. We further show that, after the suspension, investors value environmental disclosures more positively, and BIPs substantially increase environmental disclosures. Our findings highlight investor awareness as a potential policy lever for mitigating blockchain infrastructures’ environmental impacts.

detail.abstract: Agricultural modernization requires automated solutions for plant species identification to reduce manual labor and improve crop management efficiency. This work presents a deep learning framework for classifying plant seedlings into 12 species categories using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The dataset, sourced from Aarhus University in collaboration with the University of Southern Denmark, contains 4,750 RGB images of plant seedlings. A baseline CNN model was developed and subsequently enhanced through data augmentation, learning rate scheduling, and early stopping techniques. The final augmented model achieved 88.5% training accuracy, 88.8% validation accuracy, and 84.8% test accuracy with a weighted F1-score of 0.851. The model demonstrates strong classification performance across most species, with particularly high accuracy for Fat Hen (94.7%), Maize (93.6%), and Sugar beet (93.2%). These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated plant identification for agricultural applications, offering potential labor savings and improved crop management efficiency.

detail.abstract: Hemenway Falk and Tsoukalas (2026) showed that competing firms overautomate because each firm captures the full cost savings from replacing a worker while bearing only part of the demand destroyed by its layoffs. The authors treat this overautomation as a single efficiency loss. This study separates that loss into two margins, the excess automation itself and a shift of real purchasing power from workers to owners, and studies how owner spending affects each. We add one parameter, the fraction of profit that owners spend in the sector, and measure distribution by owners' real consumption share rather than by a planner's chosen weight. The central result is that the parameter that shrinks the overautomation wedge also increases the owners' real consumption share. Improving efficiency through owner spending worsens distribution because that spending returns to owners and, against fixed output, increases prices that erode workers' purchasing power. We also show that congestion in reabsorption enlarges the demand externality and that more productive AI reproduces the same tension. Correcting both the inefficiency and income shift requires an automation tax paired with redistribution, not a tax alone.

detail.abstract: Paradoxes are phenomena where the opposites appear to be at once true. When they occur in societies, they tend to precipitate resolution paralysis, or in the worst-case scenario, destruction of either or both of the involved opposites. Furthermore, paradoxes do not develop overnight or arise out of the blue. Lastly, paradoxes are often resistant to incremental trajectory-correction solutions and require paradigm shifts. Higher education in the U.S. is currently besieged by at least four paradoxes, creating a between Scylla and Charybdis1 kind of catch-22 situation, probably because it has morphed into a hard to disentangle education-industry complex. We already have an ocean of information at our disposal as the global Internet connectivity is becoming ubiquitous. Further, the dawn of the age of artificial intelligence (AI) has arrived that has a potential to make knowledge synthesis easy and trustworthy. In that context, rather than undertake an onerous task of tackling the problems in the U.S. higher education with small incremental fixes, it might be more efficient to reinvent the system totally. This white paper, enlists the paradoxes, defines the purpose of higher education, elucidates three but not the only major undercurrents that compromise education, and offers a diagnosis and a solution to the problem.

title: The Regulatory Waterbed: Unilateral Leverage Caps and the Contamination of a Shared Perpetual-Futures Settlement Index

detail.title: The Regulatory Waterbed: Unilateral Leverage Caps and the Contamination of a Shared Perpetual-Futures Settlement Index
detail.abstract: A unilateral leverage cap on perpetual-futures contracts that are cash-settled against a shared, manipulable index can raise systemic fragility while lowering total leverage and fire-sale risk. Tightening pushes leverage to opaque offshore venues, where it degrades the shared settlement price. The harm falls on onshore positions that never moved yet settle against that price. In a 2026 calibration, tightening cuts total leverage 11% and raises index contamination 22%. Risk climbs as leverage falls. Regulatory-arbitrage and macroprudential reasoning miss this referenceprice externality. No single cap can address it. The remedy is a Tinbergen pair of instruments. Clean the index, then coordinate margins.

title: Endogenous Liquidity and the Toxicity Trap: The Dynamics of Tokenized-Market Regulation

detail.title: Endogenous Liquidity and the Toxicity Trap: The Dynamics of Tokenized-Market Regulation
detail.abstract: Legitimate traders leave a tokenized market as it grows toxic. Their exit widens spreads, which drives out still more. We model this feedback as a nonlinear dynamical system. The market has two stable states. One is liquid; the other is a toxicity trap. A tipping threshold separates them. The trap is a basin of attraction with hysteresis. A market that falls in cannot escape by restoring prior enforcement. A transient enforcement surge lifts it out for good. Only the ledger can do this, not the gate. Exclusion destroys the composability that draws liquidity back. The dynamics reinforce the architecture result.

title: Hybrid Learning Practices and Their Effects on Student Learning Experiences in Ethiopian Public Universities
affiliations: , Ethiopian Civil Service University and Ethiopian Civil Service University

detail.title: Hybrid Learning Practices and Their Effects on Student Learning Experiences in Ethiopian Public Universities
detail.abstract: Hybrid learning has become an important approach to improving the quality, flexibility, and accessibility of higher education, particularly within Ethiopia's digital transformation initiative (e-SHE). This study assessed the practice of hybrid learning and its effect on students' learning experiences in Adama Science and Technology University, Jimma University, and Hawassa University. A convergent parallel mixed-methods research design was employed, combining questionnaire data from undergraduate students who had completed at least one hybrid course with focus group discussions and key informant interviews involving instructors, e-learning directors, ICT professionals, and university administrators. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Kruskal–Wallis test, Ordered Logit, Ordered Probit, and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. The findings showed that hybrid learning significantly enhanced students' learning experiences by promoting flexibility, learner autonomy, digital skill development, and active engagement. Students reported moderate to high levels of engagement and satisfaction, and significant differences in hybrid learning implementation were observed among the universities, with Adama Science and Technology University demonstrating comparatively stronger performance. Regression analyses consistently revealed that hybrid learning practice, student engagement, sustainability of hybrid learning, and student satisfaction positively and significantly influenced students' learning experiences (p < 0.01), with student satisfaction emerging as the strongest predictor. However, challenges related to instructional design, digital infrastructure, faculty preparedness, online interaction, and institutional support remain. The study concludes that strengthening digital infrastructure, faculty capacity, learner-centered instructional design, and institutional support is essential for the effective and sustainable implementation of hybrid learning in Ethiopian higher education.

title: Legislative Reform and Social Norm Change: Evidence from the Implementation of Ethiopia's Revised Family Code

detail.title: Legislative Reform and Social Norm Change: Evidence from the Implementation of Ethiopia's Revised Family Code
detail.abstract: Child marriage remains one of the most persistent barriers to gender equality and women's empowerment in many developing countries. In 2000, the Government of Ethiopia introduced the Revised Family Code (RFC), increasing the minimum legal age of marriage from 15 to 18 years and criminalizing child marriage. While legislative reform represented a significant milestone, its effectiveness depended on complementary institutional and societal interventions. This case study examines how the implementation of the Revised Family Code contributed to changing social norms surrounding child marriage in Ethiopia and identifies the key factors that facilitated or constrained its enforcement. Drawing on documentary evidence, policy reports, and existing literature, the study explores the legal, institutional, and community-level mechanisms that supported implementation. The findings reveal that the effectiveness of the Revised Family Code was initially constrained by deeply rooted cultural norms, limited institutional capacity, weak law enforcement, and inadequate access to information, particularly in rural communities. To address these challenges, the government, civil society organizations, religious institutions, and development partners implemented coordinated interventions, including nationwide awareness campaigns, community engagement initiatives, women's and girls' empowerment programs, judicial capacity building, and strengthened legal enforcement. These complementary measures contributed to shifts in public attitudes and social norms, resulting in a substantial decline in the prevalence of child marriage across Ethiopia. The study 2 concludes that legislative reform alone is insufficient to eliminate harmful traditional practices; sustained social norm transformation, institutional commitment, and community participation are essential for effective policy implementation. The findings provide valuable lessons for countries seeking to address child marriage through integrated legal and social interventions.

title: Resilience Capacity and the Determinants of Rural Household Food Security in Conflict Zones: Lessons from Nigeria

detail.abstract: It is evident that about 68.65%% of the chronically undernourished people resides in countries plagued with conflict, and this condition is exacerbated by climate-related shocks, which is the case of NorthEast Nigeria. Against this backdrop, this study determines the level of food insecurity, food resilience capacity, and the determinant factors among rural household in Borno State, Nigeria, using 160 sampled secondary data from General Household Survey (GHS), conducted by the Nigeria National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) and the World Bank (WB), collected in 2018-2019. Key findings revealed that 44% of the household in the study area are food insecure with an average food poverty intensity of 0.441, while falling short of the population's mean percapita food expenditure in the study area by 19% at P a1 , and requiring a minimum of about N 53328 to escape this vicious food insecurity embargo, while further analysis on the severity of poverty (P a2) showed that this 43% food insecure suffers an average food intensity of 0.6273 and also falls short of the population's mean per capita food expenditure in the study area by 27% poverty severity level P a2 found significant at 5% probability level. The result of the Gini coefficient analysis revealed a high food consumption expenditure inequality margin of 0.83798 among the household in the study area. The Tobit regression shows that access to aid by household negatively influences food poverty, alongside years of formal education, and found significant at 1% probabilistic level respectively. Research study-based finding polices were also proffered.

title: Can the World Cup Move Mexico City's Economy? Lessons from F1, NFL, and Major Events
affiliations: Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM)

detail.title: Can the World Cup Move Mexico City's Economy? Lessons from F1, NFL, and Major Events
detail.abstract: This working paper studies whether major event months are associated with measurable short-term changes in Mexico City's tourism and hotel market. The analysis is motivated by the 2026 FIFA World Cup, for which Mexico City Stadium is scheduled to host five matches, including the tournament's opening match. Using monthly hotel occupancy and tourist-arrival data for Mexico City from January 2019 to April 2024, I estimate whether Formula 1 and NFL event months are associated with higher hotel occupancy and tourists hosted in hotels, controlling for calendar seasonality, year effects, and the COVID-19 shock. The current results should be interpreted as preliminary conditional associations rather than causal estimates. Event months are associated with visibly higher tourism indicators in descriptive comparisons. In the main regression, Formula 1 months are associated with a 6.7 percentage-point increase in hotel occupancy, while a combined major-event indicator is associated with a 7.0 percentagepoint increase. Robustness checks keep the event coefficient positive, though statistical significance weakens when COVID-shock months are excluded. The effects on total tourists hosted in hotels are weaker and become negative after month and year controls, suggesting that occupancy captures short-run hotel-market pressure more clearly than aggregate tourist counts. The paper concludes that major events can move Mexico City's hotel market at the margin, but the magnitude and distribution of World Cup effects will depend on substitution, displacement, pricing, and whether visitors extend their stays beyond match days.

title: Are Longevity Mismatches Really Mistakes? Evidence from Subjective Survival Expectations and Future Aging Outcomes

detail.title: Are Longevity Mismatches Really Mistakes? Evidence from Subjective Survival Expectations and Future Aging Outcomes
detail.abstract: Subjective survival expectations frequently differ from actuarial survival forecasts, but it remains unclear whether these discrepancies reflect forecasting errors or information about future health risks. Using longitudinal data from the RAND Health and Retirement Study (1992-2022), this paper examines whether longevity mismatches predict subsequent aging outcomes. Individuals are classified as longevity pessimists, calibrated respondents, or longevity optimists based on the ratio of subjective to actuarial survival probabilities. The results show that longevity pessimists are significantly more likely to experience subsequent mortality, disability onset, and health deterioration, while multinomial models indicate they are less likely to experience healthy survival and more likely to transition into disability and death. Similar, though smaller, patterns are observed among longevity optimists. Overall, the findings suggest that deviations between subjective and actuarial survival expectations contain information about future aging risks beyond observable health characteristics. Rather than reflecting only miscalibration, longevity mismatches appear to provide informative signals about future health and survival trajectories.

title: The Welfare Gap Nobody Measures Psychosocial Crisis Among Nepali Migrants and the Case for Community-Based Support

detail.abstract: Nepal measures the success of labour migration almost exclusively through economic indicators-remittances, employment figures, and bilateral legal agreements. Yet across destination countries, Nepali migrants face a welfare crisis these measures do not capture: depression, addiction, suicidal ideation, isolation, and the erosion of meaning and community. Drawing on more than a decade of direct, voluntary welfare engagement with Nepali migrants in Australia and Malaysia, together with peer-reviewed evidence on migrant mental health in Gulf Cooperation Council countries, Malaysia, and the broader Asia-Pacific, this paper argues that Nepal's migration governance framework has a structural blind spot in psychosocial welfare. This gap is currently being filled, informally and at personal cost, by community figures operating without recognition, training, or institutional support. The paper documents this invisible welfare layer through case material and existing research, and proposes six specific policy reforms to acknowledge, resource, and strengthen it.

title: The Small Carry The Great: Who Is Really Funding Ukraine

detail.title: The Small Carry The Great: Who Is Really Funding Ukraine

All analysis uses publicly available, country-level aggregate data from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy's Ukraine Support Tracker (Release 29). Ethics approval is not applicable.

detail.abstract: Sixty years ago, Olson and Zeckhauser predicted that in any shared defense effort the great carry the small. In the funding of Ukraine, the prediction has failed. Working from the Kiel Institute's Ukraine Support Tracker through April 2026, I strip three distortions out of the public debate: raw totals that reward size over effort, headline pledges that overstate what has actually been allocated, and European Union aid folded into national accounts. The 41 donor governments have pledged roughly $407 billion between them, and the giving is concentrated in a way Pareto would have recognized: eight countries supply 82 percent of it. But concentration is not effort. Measured against economic size, Norway leads at 5.84 percent of its economy, while the United States, the largest donor at $136 billion, commits 0.58 percent. Among the major donors, delivery rates run from under a quarter of the pledge to 97 percent. The heaviest relative burden of this war's funding rests on the smallest shoulders, and the oldest prediction in alliance economics, that small allies free ride on great powers, holds at best conditionally. Who is really funding Ukraine turns out to be a question about arithmetic before it is a question about generosity.

title: Portfolio Optimization through Risk-averse Linear Models
affiliations: and Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)

detail.title: Portfolio Optimization through Risk-averse Linear Models
detail.abstract: We establish a novel framework for minimum deviation portfolio optimization by directly connecting a risk-averse stochastic problem (RASP) to linear regression models. By leveraging a set of coherent risk measures and scoring functions, our methodology generalizes classical models while enabling alternative formulations that account for tail risk and asymmetric scoring functions. Using S&P 100 stock data, we empirically illustrate our approach. Nonparametric hypothesis tests indicate significant differences in risk and risk-adjusted performance across RASP specifications.

title: Rubber Market Shocks, Supply-Side Risks, and Distributional Policy Responses in Thailand: A Recursive Dynamic CGE Approach
affiliations: Kasetsart University

detail.title: Rubber Market Shocks, Supply-Side Risks, and Distributional Policy Responses in Thailand: A Recursive Dynamic CGE Approach
detail.abstract: This study quantifies how rubber-sector shocks propagate through the Thai economy and distribute their welfare consequences across the income distribution, using a recursive-dynamic computable general equilibrium model calibrated to a 2024 Social Accounting Matrix and solved over 2024–2034. The central finding is a structural disproportion between macroeconomic and distributional incidence: although rubber constitutes 2.37% of national GDP, it accounts for 30% of first-quintile labour income, generating a 6.2:1 welfare loss ratio between the bottom and top quintiles under a permanent 20% price decline, while aggregate output contracts by only −0.32% — a 20:1 macro-to-household disproportion that renders national accounts surveillance systematically blind to concentrated poverty incidence. Three further asymmetries refine this picture. Negative price shocks transmit instantaneously while positive shocks face a two-to-three year absorption lag from frictional labour market rigidity. TFP deterioration generates compounding welfare losses that nearly double over the decade (Q1: −1.70% to −3.22%) through a capital-depreciation spiral with no analogue in price-shock scenarios, establishing supply-side shocks as categorically more dangerous beyond a two-year horizon. Export demand contractions produce an inverted distributional gradient — upper quintiles lose more than lower — revealing that capital income exposure to downstream processing, not farm-gate price exposure, governs trade-shock incidence. Among three policy instruments, a targeted cash transfer (≈0.06% of GDP) delivers superior welfare efficiency per unit of fiscal expenditure relative to a production subsidy; phased productivity investment dominates both in long-run present-value terms but provides no short-run relief. The social discount rate is therefore the pivotal parameter in instrument choice, and the 20:1 macro-to-household disproportion the pivotal argument for replacing GDP-threshold monitoring with household-panel early-warning systems in commodity-dependent economies.

title: A "Non-Guessing" Theory for How to Process Information
affiliations: University of Vienna - Department of Economics

detail.title: A "Non-Guessing" Theory for How to Process Information
detail.abstract: We introduce a new theory, founded with axioms, for how to use information when making choices under uncertainty. The objective referred to as non-guessing is to perform better with information than without it, in the true state, where performance without information is evaluated using a given mixed action. A Bayesian does not have this property as they only care about doing well in a state that is drawn from their prior. Our criterion embeds unbiased hypothesis testing when there are only two actions. We investigate informativeness, evaluate frequentist heuristics and show in numerous settings how to optimally use data.

title: Integrating Infectious Disease Regulation into Natural Capital Accounting: Gaps, Challenges, and Opportunities

detail.abstract: Ecosystem integrity and infectious disease risk have attracted greater attention since the COVID pandemic, amid rising concerns about biodiversity loss and environmental degradation. Natural ecosystems regulate disease transmission through ecological mechanisms that shape host diversity, vector populations, and wildlife-human interactions. However, natural capital accounting frameworks poorly represent these health benefits. This article explores how to integrate the ecosystem service of infectious disease regulation into natural capital accounting. Using the ecosystem service cascade model and the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA-EA) framework, we propose a conceptual approach that links ecosystem condition, service capacity, disease regulation flows, and economic benefits. The paper reviews ecological mechanisms linking environmental change and disease emergence, discusses methods for valuing disease regulation services, and identifies key methodological challenges with causal inference, spatial scale, and economic valuation. Integrating infectious disease regulation into ecosystem accounting can support preventive policy development, guide land-use planning, and strengthen the role of ecosystem conservation in public health protection and economic resilience.

title: The Centralization Paradox: How Authoritarian Reforms Reproduce Patronage through Spatial Capture
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), New York University (NYU) - Department of Politics and

detail.title: The Centralization Paradox: How Authoritarian Reforms Reproduce Patronage through Spatial Capture
detail.abstract: Despite formidable enforcement capacity, authoritarian regimes frequently find their centralization reforms yield mixed results. This article theorizes a centralization paradox: reforms intended to curb corruption and strengthen control instead shift power upward and reproduce patronage at higher administrative levels. We advance a novel mechanism of spatial capture, in which politically reliant firms adapt to the loss of local protection by reallocating investment to rebuild patronage ties under newly centralized authority. We locate our theory in China’s 2014 judicial reform, which centralized court authority at the provincial level. Combining a difference-in-differences specification with a shift–share design, we show that politically reliant firms withdrew from reformed jurisdictions and reinvested in provincial capitals, where concentrated authority revitalized patronage. The findings reveal an endogenous limit on centralization reforms: with weak institutions, reforms meant to purge local collusion instead relocate it, reproducing patronage in new political geographies.

title: How Plan Design Shapes the Value of Managed Accounts
affiliations: Morningstar Center for Retirement and Policy Studies and Morningstar, Inc. - Morningstar Investment Management LLC

detail.title: How Plan Design Shapes the Value of Managed Accounts
detail.abstract: Managed accounts can deliver meaningful value for defined contribution plan participants, and this analysis shows where that value is likely to be greatest. Using Morningstar's Defined Contribution Outcomes Model, or DCOM, we examine how default contribution rates, auto-escalation, and employer matching shape the incremental gains managed accounts can provide when controlling for participant age, wage, and tenure. The results show that managed accounts can improve retirement outcomes across a wide range of plan environments. Their impact is largest when participant behavior is less influenced by plan design, such as in plans with lower default contribution rates, no auto-escalation, and greater reliance on individual decision-making. In more structured plans, managed accounts still provide value, but the incremental opportunity is generally smaller because automatic features already place many participants on stronger savings trajectories. Rather than asking only whether managed accounts add value, plan sponsors may want to ask where they add the most value and how they should be deployed. This analysis provides a practical framework for answering that question.

title: Bond Portfolio Optimization
affiliations: Amundi Institute, Amundi Institute, Amundi Asset Management and Amundi Asset Management

detail.title: Bond Portfolio Optimization
detail.abstract:
Although bond portfolio optimization is one of the oldest applications of the mean-variance framework, it is considerably less developed and adopted than its equity and multi-asset counterparts. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for bond portfolio optimization applied to investment universes composed of individual securities. We first identify the challenges that distinguish bond portfolio optimization from equity portfolio optimization. We then develop a family of optimization problems with and without a benchmark under alternative risk factor models. In particular, we focus on a two-factor risk model based on interest rates and credit risk. We also distinguish between L1-norm and L2-norm optimization problems, and show how these formulations can be cast into linear programming and quadratic programming problems using the properties of quadratic and extended linear forms. Beyond these standard formulations, we consider advanced optimization problems combining both L1 and L2 risk measures. We pay particular attention to active share constraints, which play a central role in fixed-income portfolio management. 

The second part of the paper is dedicated to empirical applications using the ICE BofA Corporate Bond indices (Global, EUR, and USD). We first illustrate the differences between L1-norm and L2-norm optimization and their impact on tracking error volatility. We then apply the Barra multi-factor risk model and decompose portfolio risk into common factor and specific risk contributions. The third application addresses active portfolio management, where we decompose expected excess returns into carry, rolldown, and repricing components. The fourth application considers the classical problem of portfolio decarbonization. The fifth application examines the sensitivity of portfolio construction to alternative clustering and bucketing methodologies. The sixth and final application illustrates the practical challenges of constructing investable portfolios and demonstrates that the difference between model and investable portfolios is a primary issue in fixed-income optimization.

detail.abstract: We propose the Soft-Min Cobb-Douglas (SMCD) matching function, a tractable threeparameter specication satisfying four desiderata: smoothness and concavity, constant returns to scale, exact joint calibration to any target market tightness, job-nding rate, and matching elasticity, and bounded matching probabilities f, q ∈ (0, 1) for all market tightness. Cobb-Douglas fails to satisfy the probability bounds, and the Den HaanRameyWatson (HRW) function cannot independently target both level and elasticity. Bounded probabilities imply a strictly decreasing matching elasticity and, through the Hosios condition, a countercyclical eciency wedge: excess unemployment rises in recessions, a mechanism Cobb-Douglas conceals and HRW mismeasures. We extend SMCD to a two-plateau variant (2P-SMCD) allowing the curvature parameter to dier across the vacancy-scarce and worker-scarce regimes, adding exactly one free parameter while preserving all four properties. Estimating all specications on U.S. monthly data from 1951 to 2025, we detect a structural break in matching eciency in October 2008. In pre-and post-break horse races, the single-p SMCD strictly dominates HRW in t while respecting probability bounds by construction. Cobb-Douglas achieves lower unconditional RMSE but does so by violating q ≤ 1 in 12 and 9 percent of pre-and post-break months, respectively. 2P-SMCD ts as well as CD in the months in which latter constitutes a valid probability model.

title: The British Patient: The Geography of Power, a Constitutional Malady, and a Diagnosis Beyond Left and Right — The Territorial Monopolisation of State Capacity and the Fiscal Conditions of Devolution
affiliations: Strategic Policy Research, Inc.

detail.title: The British Patient: The Geography of Power, a Constitutional Malady, and a Diagnosis Beyond Left and Right — The Territorial Monopolisation of State Capacity and the Fiscal Conditions of Devolution
detail.abstract:
Britain's regional inequality is among the widest in the developed world, and its governing dysfunction is conventionally attributed to "centralisation." This monograph argues that the diagnosis is mistaken. Centralisation as such is not the disease—France is highly centralised yet sustains responsive regions—and the true pathology is the territorial monopolisation of state capacity: the simultaneous concentration, at a single centre, of fiscal, administrative, and decision-making capacity. Through comparison with France, Germany, and the United States, and a sustained study of Greater Manchester, the book shows that Britain is anomalous in monopolising all three dimensions at once, and that London is not merely the extractive centre but is itself a prisoner of the same architecture.

It then theorises why the arrangement persists. Reform requires the very institution that holds capacity to surrender it, so that, within ordinary politics, no actor can advance reform without weakening the institutional position from which they act—a self-locking centralisation, deepened by a capacity-extraction cycle in which the periphery's induced incapacity becomes the justification for further extraction. The book identifies the conditions under which the lock can open, and argues that fiscal autonomy is decisive—not because localities need more money, but because governing capacity cannot be granted, only generated through fiscal responsibility. The prescription pairs dispersed fiscal capacity with rule-based equalisation, on the German rather than the American model, and shows that liberating the periphery would also liberate London.

A reading of the June 2026 British leadership transition—the rival devolution platforms of Andy Burnham and the Conservative opposition—shows the framework at work on live constitutional politics: both leave the fiscal lock shut, the one by omission, the other by design. A general model is proposed, of which Britain appears a particularly clear instance.

title: Image Considerations in Second-Hand Adoption: A Vignette Experiment
affiliations: University of Insubria - Department of Economics, Universität Innsbruck and University of Rome Tor Vergata

detail.title: Image Considerations in Second-Hand Adoption: A Vignette Experiment

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite growing recognition that image considerations underlie the adoption of secondhand goods, research in this domain has largely overlooked the possibility that different image dimensions operate through distinct channels. Using a vignette experiment on a nationally representative Italian sample (N = 10; 496), this paper disentangles the effects of three image perspectives – self-image, social image, and second-order self-image (beliefs about others’ self-image) – across four main dimensions of secondhand adoption: financial, social, environmental, and hygiene. Contrary to findings in other behavioral domains, self-image emerges as the stronger predictor of intention to adopt second-hand, with the largest gaps over social image for hygiene and social-approval dimensions and the smallest – though still significant – for environmental considerations. Within self-image, hygiene and financial considerations are the strongest correlates of adoption, while environmental consciousness is the weakest; yet it becomes relevant under other-oriented perspectives (social and second-order), suggesting it operates more as a social signal than a private value. Participants also systematically underestimate how positively others view themselves when engaging in second-hand adoption, and this underestimation depresses adoption intentions more than overestimation boosts them – a pattern consistent with pluralistic ignorance that may act as a self-reinforcing barrier to adoption.

title: Semiconductor Tariffs as Policy Whiplash

detail.abstract: We study the risk-taking behavior of asset managers delegated by institutional investors through separately managed accounts, a setting in which mandate-retention concerns are particularly salient relative to compensation incentives. Using a hand-collected dataset of Italian occupational pension funds over the period 2003-2023, we find that managers adopt more conservative investment strategies when mandates are larger, when the same mandate is assigned to multiple competing managers, and as contracts approach expiration. These patterns are consistent with managers adjusting their behavior to preserve the mandate and reduce termination risk rather than to maximize current compensation. Our findings have implications for the design of delegated investment mandates and the incentive structures faced by professional asset managers.

title: Introduction To Currency Wars

detail.title: Introduction To Currency Wars
detail.abstract: The phenomenon of currency wars is defined as the competitive devaluation of national currencies to gain trade and growth advantages. Tracing their evolution from the Great Depression through the Bretton Woods collapse, the Plaza Accord, the Asian Financial Crisis, the Global Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic, the study highlights how economic shocks often trigger aggressive exchange rate interventions. The mechanisms of devaluation ranging from foreign exchange interventions and reserve accumulation to interest rate policies and capital controls are analyzed alongside their domestic and global repercussions, such as inflation, trade tensions, and market instability. The research also reviews the international legal frameworks governing currency manipulation, including the IMF Articles of Agreement, U.S. legislation, and OECD provisions, while underscoring their limitations in enforcement. Finally, the paper considers the role of cryptocurrencies and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), which are reshaping monetary competition and challenging the dominance of traditional reserve currencies. The study concludes that while devaluation remains a powerful but destabilizing economic tool, sustainable solutions require stronger multilateral cooperation, transparent policies, and adaptation to emerging digital financial systems.

detail.abstract: On February 16, 1968, a red telephone rang inside a police station in Haleyville, Alabama. A congressman answered. The call lasted seconds. But what it started changed American public safety forever. That single call, placed 35 days after AT&T announced the concept, launched the most consequential emergency infrastructure system the modern world has ever built. Today, 9-1-1 handles roughly 240 million calls per year across 5,748 Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs). Police, fire, and emergency medical services converge through a single unified number that has become the operational backbone of American public safety. More than 82 percent of those calls now originate from wireless devices, a complete reversal from the system's landline origins and a transformation that has demanded continuous infrastructure evolution. This report traces the full arc of 911: from its 1968 origins through the Enhanced 911 (E911) era, the wireless revolution, the copper sunset crisis, and into Next Generation 911 (NG911) built on broadband IP and ESInet architecture. It examines how 911 integrates police, fire, and EMS under a single dispatch framework; how VoIP and cybersecurity threats are reshaping the system's risk profile; and how emerging technologies including AI, satellite connectivity, and predictive dispatch are extending what emergency response can do. It also confronts the system's most urgent human problem: a deepening staffing crisis across every emergency discipline. Dispatcher vacancy rates of 25 to 30 percent, paramedic shortages in rural markets, and volunteer fire department attrition are straining the human layer that no technology can fully replace. This report examines the training pipelines, the AI tools that serve as force multipliers, and the public-private partnership models that are beginning to close the gap. It recognizes the emergency management officials, PSAP directors, state 911 coordinators, and federal agency staff who architect and maintain the system behind the system: the people who manage funding battles, NG911 procurement, cybersecurity defense, and disaster response without pause, in the service of a promise that America makes to every resident within its borders. Key findings: every minute without defibrillation in a cardiac arrest reduces survival by 7-10%; structure fires caused $14.7 billion in property losses in 2023; California's $450 million NG911 program was scrapped in 2025 and restarted, illustrating the transition's difficulty; FirstNet now connects 37,000 public safety agencies; and the FCC's NG911 rules took full effect November 2024, setting the legal framework for the decade ahead.

title: Beyond Rational Choice: Why Economic Behaviour Cannot Be Understood Without Neurobiology, Culture, And Historical Trauma

detail.title: Beyond Rational Choice: Why Economic Behaviour Cannot Be Understood Without Neurobiology, Culture, And Historical Trauma
detail.abstract: The rational choice model-homo economicus making consistent, utility-maximising decisions from stable, exogenous preferences-is the foundational assumption of mainstream economics. This paper argues that this assumption is not merely incomplete but structurally incorrect in ways that generate systematic policy failures, particularly in developing economies with histories of institutional trauma and strong communal cultural frameworks. Drawing on convergent evidence from neuroscience, anthropology, and development economics, and grounded in the Neuro-Anthropological Leadership Model (NALM) developed through doctoral research in Nederburg, Western Cape, South Africa, this paper makes five arguments that collectively constitute a case for replacing rational choice as economics' foundational model.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the comparative effectiveness of Canada's two principal federal carbon-pricing instruments - the Federal Fuel Charge (FFC) and the Output-Based Pricing System (OBPS) - in reducing greenhouse gas emissions between 2021 and 2025. The period is analytically unusual: both instruments were calibrated to an identical minimum carbon price from 2019 to 2024, before the Government of Canada eliminated the FFC's consumer-facing rate to zero on 1 April 2025 while retaining and committing to strengthen the OBPS. Drawing on Pigouvian tax theory, marginal abatement cost heterogeneity, and Weitzman's (1974) prices-versus-quantities framework, the paper argues that the conventional price-versus-quantity framing fits Canada poorly, since neither instrument imposes a binding emissions cap; the more relevant distinction is tax base and incidence. Using emissions data, price-trajectory evidence, Parliamentary Budget Officer distributional analysis, Canadian Climate Institute policy-attribution modelling, and the British Columbia carbon tax literature as the closest causal analogue, the paper finds that industrial carbon pricing is consistently projected to deliver a substantially larger share of abatement than the consumer levy, but that this evidence is heavily confounded by post-pandemic recovery, energy-price shocks, continuous National Inventory Report revisions, provincial policy heterogeneity, and overlapping regulation. The OBPS's greater political durability is shown to coexist with a documented weak-price-signal problem in at least one major provincial-equivalent credit market, while the FFC's well-evidenced behavioural effectiveness was foreclosed by its 2025 cancellation. The paper concludes that OBPS-style pricing has been the larger, but not unambiguously superior, contributor to Canadian carbon-pricing effectiveness, and proposes a difference-in-differences exploitation of the 2025 policy reversal as a route to sharper causal identification.

detail.abstract: Public-health interventions often aspire to generate spillovers beyond the households they directly reach, but identifying who is exposed to whom within communities is challenging. Researchers frequently approximate social exposure using geographic proximity, even though the individuals who transmit health advice need not be nearby. We study this issue by conducting secondary analysis of a randomized maternal and child health counseling intervention in rural Honduras with geocoded households and mapped social networks. At our main 50-meter radius, geographic proximity captures only 30.8% of health-advice ties, while only 3.7% of geographically proximate household pairs are connected by advice-giving. The choice of exposure mapping matters for what the analysis detects. Exposure mappings based solely on geographic proximity yield a precise zero effect on diarrhea knowledge. By contrast, exposure through advice ties beyond 50 meters increases diarrhea knowledge, and the effect is statistically distinguishable from exposure through nearby non-advice contacts. The evidence suggests that simple, actionable illness-management knowledge diffuses through advice relationships that geographic proximity alone fails to capture. Reported diarrhea, indicating whether the respondent or any child had diarrhea in the previous four weeks, also increases with advice exposure outside 50m, consistent with greater recognition, recall, or reporting rather than higher underlying morbidity. We find no corresponding effects for respiratory knowledge or reported respiratory illness. Our results show that using geographic proximity as a proxy for social exposure can mask important channels of information transmission and could lead researchers to miss meaningful spillover effects.
