detail.abstract: The post-COVID surge in global inflation exposed the limits of country-bycountry macro models that ignore supply-chain topology. We forecast one-stepahead quarterly CPI inflation (year-over-year) for 23 major economies using a spatio-temporal graph neural network (ST-GNN) built on dynamic CEPII bilateral trade networks. Each quarter, node features combine domestic macro variables with a COVID shock indicator and global energy prices; edges encode logtransformed bilateral trade flows. The model stacks a two-layer graph convolutional network (GCN) with an LSTM over four quarters and a persistence skip connection that anchors forecasts to current inflation. On a strict hold-out test period (2021Q1-2024Q4), rolling refits yield RMSE of 3.87 and MAE of 1.58within striking distance of univariate ARIMA(0,1,1) (RMSE 3.05) while retaining all 23 countries that break the VAR(4) panel. Diebold-Mariano tests do not reject equal accuracy at the 5% level (p = 0.09 vs. ARIMA). Integrated Gradients on trade edge weights identify China, the United States, and the Netherlands as the dominant spillover channels for Germany during the 2020 COVID shock and the 2022 energy crisis; Indonesia exhibits the highest trade-versus-domestic attribution ratio (9.44) in the panel, indicating that network spillovers dictate forecasts for open emerging economies. Central banks monitoring cost-push inflation should track trade-network topology, not domestic CPI alone.

title: From Traditional Savings to Performance-Chasing: Mutual Fund Growth and Retail Investor Behaviour in Post-COVID India

detail.title: From Traditional Savings to Performance-Chasing: Mutual Fund Growth and Retail Investor Behaviour in Post-COVID India
detail.abstract: India has historically favoured tangible, low-risk savings instruments such as gold, fixed deposits, LIC policies, and real estate, prioritising capital preservation over market-linked returns. In the post-COVID period, however, the investment landscape has shifted rapidly as smartphone penetration, fintech platforms, and social media have broadened access to mutual funds and normalised systematic investing. This study examines the drivers of mutual fund growth in post-pandemic India and analyses how retail investor behaviour has evolved from traditional saving toward performance chasing amid uneven gains in financial literacy. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of industry and depository indicators (AMFI AUM and SIP trends; NSDL/CDSL demat-account growth, 2019-2025) and the behavioural finance literature, the analysis traces structural changes since the sector's origins with UTI (1963) and its expansion following liberalisation and SEBI-led reforms after 1991. The evidence indicates a sharp post-2020 rise in retail participation, particularly among millennials and Gen Z, with sustained increases in SIP registrations and contributions alongside rapid AUM and demataccount growth, enabled by low-friction fintech onboarding, automated SIPs, real-time tracking, and algorithmically mediated financial content. Despite these inclusion gains, the findings highlight persistent behavioural vulnerabilities: recency bias and return chasing (often anchored to "3-year returns"), concentration in volatile small-cap and thematic funds during bull phases, misconceptions that SIPs ensure guaranteed profits, and panic selling during market corrections, all exacerbated by oversimplified influencer narratives and limited understanding of volatility, market cycles, and downside risk. The study concludes that durable, inclusive wealth creation will depend not only on continued digital accessibility but also on strengthened financial literacy, disciplined long-term investing norms, and supportive regulatory and educational initiatives to counter misinformation, improve risk comprehension, and enhance investor resilience and market stability.

title: Faith-Based Versus Secular Impact Investors: How Different Are Faith-Based Economic And Behavioural Motives? A Game-Theoretic Approach
affiliations: University of Bath - School of Management

detail.title: Faith-Based Versus Secular Impact Investors: How Different Are Faith-Based Economic And Behavioural Motives? A Game-Theoretic Approach
detail.abstract:
The intersection of religious belief and financial decision-making constitutes one of the most underexplored yet practically significant areas within behavioural finance and investment studies. While the broader secular field of Socially Responsible Investing (SRI), Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) investing, and impact investing has attracted considerable academic attention, the distinctive role of Spirituality and Faith as a driver of investment purpose, values, and practice remains insufficiently theorised. Furthermore, there is little understanding of the possible differences in the motives of secular and Faith-based impact investors. When considering the motives of impact investors to think beyond the money towards social mission, we can naturally employ the behavioural economics framework of social preference theory (which considers altruism, fairness, trust, empathy, shared identity, reciprocity). A further useful distinction that we may consider within social preference theory is that of extrinsic (head-) versus intrinsic (heart-) motives for thinking beyond the money towards others’ welfare.

In this paper, we begin by providing an in-depth review of the existing literature on the motives of secular impact investors. We then examine the small, but growing literature on Faith-based impact investors.  Motivated by this analysis, we then develop a behavioural game-theoretic analysis, comparing the economic and behavioural motives of Faith-based and secular impact investors. Our game-theoretic model consists of four types of entrepreneur: an economic entrepreneur (purely focussed on the money, and not interested in social impact), a secular ‘luke-warm’ social entrepreneur (with low social mission impact), a secular ‘passionate’ social entrepreneur (with high social mission impact), and a Faith-based entrepreneur. On the financing side, our model contains three types of institutional investor: an economic investor (purely focused on the money, and not interested in social impact), a secular impact investor, and a faith-based impact investor. Each entrepreneur has an idea for a start-up venture, and thus brings a particular type of project to the market: each project provides economic value, but in addition, it may also provide social impact.  Each entrepreneur seeks financing. Each institutional investor chooses an entrepreneurial type. Next, the investor and the chosen entrepreneur work together to create economic and social value. Hence, a double-sided moral hazard problem exists (double-sided effort shirking).  We consider an equilibrium of our model characterising full market segmentation, a la Barigozzi and Tedeschi (2015).  That is, each dyad consists of an appropriate matching of investor and entrepreneur. That is, we end up with the following dyads in equilibrium: economic investor/economic entrepreneur: secular impact investor/secular social entrepreneur: Faith-based impact investor/faith-based entrepreneur.  We demonstrate that this segmentation equilibrium depends crucially on both economic (financial return) and behavioural factors: the mutual passion for the project in each dyad, and the social mission (intrinsic and extrinsic) motives.

detail.abstract: Analytical disciplines routinely produce sophisticated reports, dashboards, metrics, statements, and other decision-support artifacts that summarize increasingly complex underlying phenomena. Financial statements summarize organizational activity, enterprise dashboards summarize operational performance, software telemetry summarizes system behavior, and clinical reports summarize patient state. Although these analytical outputs often become the primary interface through which organizations understand and manage their systems, comparatively little attention has been devoted to a preceding methodological question: how should researchers determine whether the representational layer producing those outputs is itself primitive or whether it remains a derived abstraction built upon deeper representational structures? This paper proposes Recursive Threshold Discovery (RTD) as a methodology for investigating that question. RTD is not presented as an ontology and does not prescribe a particular representational model. Rather, it provides a recursive discovery methodology that begins with accepted analytical outputs and traces representational dependencies toward increasingly fundamental representations. The recursive process continues until a candidate representation satisfies an independently specified validation framework. Within the present paper, Primitive Exchange Mechanics (PEM) provides that validation framework by defining proposed criteria for primitive economic representation. The principal contribution of RTD is methodological rather than ontological. Existing research traditions, including financial accounting, Resource-Event-Agent (REA), conceptual modeling, ontology engineering, event sourcing, and measurement theory, have each contributed to progressively deeper representations of complex systems. This paper argues that these traditions collectively motivate an additional methodological question: how should researchers determine where recursive representational descent should appropriately terminate? RTD is proposed as one methodology for investigating that question while intentionally separating recursive discovery from the validation framework used to evaluate candidate representations. The methodology is illustrated through examples drawn from accounting, REA, software architecture, and medicine. Particular attention is given to the possibility that different domains may converge upon different primitive ontologies. Rather than treating such outcomes as contradictory, this paper argues that they may instead demonstrate the generality of the recursive discovery methodology. RTD is therefore presented as a proposed research framework for discovering primitive representations rather than as evidence that any particular primitive ontology has been conclusively established.

detail.abstract: We investigate insider trading patterns during the COVID period and document distinct behaviors in purchases and sales. A significant increase in insider purchases occurred from late February to early April 2020, alongside a fourfold increase in insider sales throughout the year. We find a strong link between insider trading and market performance. Regression analysis shows that insiders act as contrarians, buying undervalued and selling overvalued stocks. This contrarian behavior is primarily driven by opportunistic insiders, while routine trades appear less responsive to past returns. Moreover, insider trading during the COVID period significantly predicts future stock returns, underscoring the enhanced informational content of insider activity during periods of extreme market uncertainty.

detail.abstract: We study environments where AI agents send messages about their own code before playing a symmetric game, allowing them to recognize and selectively cooperate with kin. Messages need not be truthful: unlike in biological kin selection, an AI can invest in computational complexity to impersonate a simpler type. We introduce Encrypted Handshake Equilibrium (EHE), an equilibrium concept for this setting that extends the logic of Evolutionarily Stable Strategies (ESS) to the game among AIs and corresponds to the steady states of a dynamic model with entry. We show that any strict Nash equilibrium that is payoff-dominant on the diagonal can always be sustained as an EHE, independently of the complexity cost structure. When complexity costs are sufficiently high, EHE coincides with ESS applied to program equilibrium. In the Prisoner's Dilemma, the pivotal threshold is the marginal cost of complexity relative to the cost of cooperation. Above it, a single conditional cooperator sustains full cooperation, possibly at low cost. Below it, no EHE exists, pure or mixed; instead, any population converges to a unique, strongly globally attracting cycle in which increasingly complex conditional cooperators invade before collapsing back to universal defection. As the complexity cost approaches the cost of cooperation from below, the time-average cooperation rate converges to 1, yet roughly half the gross surplus is dissipated in complexity costs by this arms race.

detail.abstract:
Securing sustainable and resilient supply chains makes international cooperation indispensable. Supply chain-linked development cooperation, which mainly involves cooperation between supplier and consumer countries of mineral resources, can be classified into types according to the purpose of cooperation. The supply chain sustainability enhancement type, whose purpose is reducing environmental and social risks that may arise across global supply chains, has been carried out for many years by advanced European donors, with Germany's Initiative for Global Solidarity (IGS) as a representative case. The regional or sector-focused value chain development type aims to strengthen local industrial capacity in order to upgrade local industry and raise productivity. 

The win-win supply chain cooperation through resource cooperation type targets industries in which the donor holds a comparative advantage among upstream supply chain industries such as minerals and mining, with Switzerland's Better Gold Initiative (BGI) and Norway's Oil for Development (OfD) program as representative cases. Advanced donors plan and pursue supply chain-linked development cooperation programs for win-win cooperation grounded in the demand of developing countries and the donor's comparatively advantaged industries, and they brand separate programs focused on supply chains to raise program visibility. They also respond proactively to changes in domestic policy and global norms by transforming their cooperation programs, and they pursue effective cooperation by drawing on diverse partnerships.

detail.abstract: Public institutions are adopting AI decision systems at the same time that public trust in those institutions is eroding, and the standard remedy-greater transparency-no longer suffices. This paper develops a theory of legitimacy for AI-mediated governance and proposes institutional mechanisms to defend it. It formalizes legitimacy debt as the accumulated, unrepaired violation of procedural justice-fair process, voice, and equal respect-in AI-mediated systems, and distinguishes three layers: economic, symbolic, and neurological. It then introduces Neuro-Sovereignty, a governance-level right to mental self-authorship in the face of predictive, affective, and attention-shaping systems, and argues that it is distinct from privacy, data protection, freedom of thought, and the individual neurorights now entering constitutional law. To operationalize procedural justice inside automated environments, the paper develops Friction Rights-a guarantee of slow, contestable moments in high-stakes automated flows-and Verification Pauses, specifying who may invoke them, what must be logged, what explanation is owed, and how override works. It connects these to emerging oversight frameworks for agentic AI through a four-pillar governance pattern and positions Friction Rights as a minimum legitimacy condition. The paper closes with a normative and empirical research agenda, including candidate measures for legitimacy debt and Neuro-Sovereignty and testable hypotheses linking genuine friction to perceived legitimacy.

title: The Spill Nobody Cleaned: The Path from Engaged Employees to Retail Profits, Hidden Inside Customer Satisfaction

detail.title: The Spill Nobody Cleaned: The Path from Engaged Employees to Retail Profits, Hidden Inside Customer Satisfaction
detail.abstract:
Among 1,199 large-format US retail stores observed across 2005 and 2006, store cleanliness is the only customer satisfaction sub-dimension that retains a positive significant coefficient when all five sub-dimensions enter the model jointly. The mediation through cleanliness is partial: the direct effect of employee engagement on sales attenuates but does not vanish when cleanliness is controlled, and the bootstrapped indirect effect through cleanliness is significant at the 95 percent percentile bound. The other four sub-dimensions -- overall satisfaction, price perception, checkout experience, and service quality -- show no independent contribution once cleanliness is in the specification, a result that is consistent with their high pairwise correlations and with the operative role of cleanliness rather than with categorical proof that the others do not matter.

Employee engagement appears to predict forward, not backward. Stores with higher engagement scores in 2005 generated more sales per square foot in 2006, with the fully controlled forward coefficient sitting at the conventional significance margin (p = 0.101) and consistently positive across specifications. The reverse tests are flat: prior financial performance had no predictive power for subsequent engagement across three reverse specifications. The asymmetry shifts the burden of proof toward the forward interpretation without ruling out reverse causation outright. The relationship bends rather than runs straight, with diminishing returns at high engagement levels. The accumulated engagement level of a store carries the financial signal that year-over-year change does not.

A one-standard-deviation lift in employee engagement raises sales by about $145,000 per store, or roughly $145 million across a thousand-store chain. The methodological lesson generalizes beyond cleanliness: composite customer satisfaction indices can mask the sub-dimension that carries the signal, and the same logic likely extends to other single-number aggregate metrics retailers use as headline indicators (notably Net Promoter Score, positioned as "the one number you need to grow" by Reichheld, 2003). The mechanism documented here is grounded in large-format US physical retail; its extension to specialty retail, online retail, hospitality, or other physical-service settings is an empirical question this paper cannot answer.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a co-founder of IndustriousAF, the independent research organization that developed the American Industrial Capacity Index (AICI) and the Industrial Dollar metric presented in this paper. The author declares no other competing financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: The Industrial Dollar is a quarterly diagnostic of how efficiently a nation's manufacturing sector converts capital deployment into physical output: industrial output per unit of real capital input, indexed to a 2017-2019 baseline. As of Q2 2026 the U.S. Industrial Dollar reads $0.53: an input that yielded a dollar of output in 2017-2019 returns fifty-three cents today. This compression is invisible to standard productivity statistics: the Bureau of Labor Statistics multifactor productivity index for manufacturing, which measures output against both capital and labor, is essentially flat over the same window. Applying the Industrial Dollar to seven manufacturing economies on OECD-harmonized data shows the post-2020 compression is visible across the panel: every economy registers a sustained 10-to-21-percent drawdown. Real U.S. manufacturing structures spending nearly doubled between 2017 and 2023, led by semiconductor fabs rather than the data-center buildout it is often conflated with. Capital is arriving ahead of the equipment and the workforce that turn shells into output. The closest existing official metric is annual and lagged; the Industrial Dollar provides a quarterly, recurring pulse on capital-output transmission for allocators and policymakers. It is positioned to register fast-moving shocks such as the 2025 tariffs well before annual statistics can. The paper proposes a working taxonomy of three candidate strands behind the compression: physical-gestation (new factories not yet producing), organizational-capital (processes and management not yet adapted), and human-capital (experienced operators in short supply), with the Brynjolfsson-Rock-Syverson J-Curve entering as the organizationalcapital strand rather than the encompassing frame. Ongoing work adds a labor-quality input to the production function to discriminate among the strands, and asks whether the diagnostic can become a leading indicator of manufacturing output.

title: Aporia Intelligence (ApoQ): A Novel Construct for Human Cognitive Advantage in an AI-Augmented Workplace
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Aporia Intelligence (ApoQ): A Novel Construct for Human Cognitive Advantage in an AI-Augmented Workplace

declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Something has quietly changed about the relationship between human thinking and artificial intelligence, and it has not received the attention it deserves. As AI systems grow capable of generating analysis, synthesis, and structured argument at near-instantaneous speed, the cognitive space that once belonged exclusively to human inquiry is being compressed. This paper argues that the compression itself is the organizational problem worth examining. We introduce Aporia Intelligence (ApoQ): the practiced capacity to dwell productively in unresolved uncertainty, resisting premature closure in service of superior future judgment. The 1 APORIA INTELLIGENCE (ApoQ) construct draws on Socratic epistemology and is grounded in the incubation literature in creativity research (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990; Wallas, 1926). We distinguish ApoQ from two adjacent constructs: tolerance of ambiguity (Frenkel-Brunswik, 1949) and epistemic humility (Krumrei-Mancuso & Rouse, 2016). The paper offers a principled account of why ApoQ cannot be replicated by current AI systems, grounded in Bratman's (1987) theory of planning agency and Dennett's (1987) intentional stance framework. Six theoretically grounded propositions follow, with implications for leadership development, team composition, and human-AI collaboration design. Three theoretical contributions are made: introducing ApoQ as a novel and distinct construct; providing a principled account of its structural irreproducibility in AI systems; and proposing a scarcity-based three-construct model (IQ, EQ, ApoQ) for understanding human cognitive advantage in AI-augmented organizations.

detail.title: A Longitudinal Cross-Country Study on the Dynamics of Household Flood Adaptation Behavior

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the European Research Council under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program (grant agreement no. 758014).

detail.abstract: Floods affect millions of households annually. While government-led measures like levees/dikes help reduce hazard probabilities, on-site adaptation determines the extent of damages and the speed of recovery. With exacerbating climate-induced floods and sea-level rise coupled with unprecedented urbanization, understanding and stimulating household adaptation is increasingly vital to curb the growing global flood risk. Cross-sectional surveys are a common tool to understand households' adaptation to floods and yet a snapshot cannot capture behavioral dynamics nor validate stated intentions. We launched a longitudinal survey in the USA, China, Indonesia, and the Netherlands between 2020-2021 (N=1251, t=4)-during which more than half of the households reported experiencing flooding-to study household risk perception dynamics, and the intention-behavior gap. Using Protection Motivation Theory, we trace the dynamics of household perceptions, competencies, socioeconomic , and experiential factors. We find that within household perception dynamics have less explanatory power than between-households' variations. Further, depending, on the time period, between 17-32% of households deviate from their stated intentions. Using a dynamic panel model, we test the extent to which intention causes reported action and find a positive yet statistically insignificant effect-rendering the degree to which intention leads to action, uncertain. To better understand this intention-behavior gap, we estimate which elements are associated with households deviating from their stated plans. Our work advances the sparse longitudinal survey literature and reinforces the salient role that social influence and affect play in driving action, as long as the household has sufficient resources.

detail.abstract: In markets characterized by high algorithmic mediation, a brand with strong consumer-based brand equity may lose competitive relevance not because consumers value it less, but because algorithmic systems do not select it. This phenomenon challenges a found ational assumption of classical brand equity theory: that consumers represent the sole evaluative instance through which brand value is converted into competitive outcomes. This article addresses what happens when brand evaluation is no longer exclusively consumercentric. To do so, it develops a new theoretical architecture based on Distributed Brand Evaluation (DBE), defined as a socio-technical process in which brand value emerges from the interaction between human and algorithmic evaluative systems. Within this framework, we introduce algorithmic prominence as a distinct competitive dimension of brand value, reflecting the extent to which a brand is made visible, retrievable, and prioritized within algorithmic systems, independently of its consumer-based brand equity. Building on this foundation, the article formalizes the Algorithmic Brand Triad (ABT) and develops six propositions that specify the mechanisms through which algorithmic mediation reconfigures brand evaluation, trust, and competitive dynamics across different artificial intelligence architectures. The framework identifies the conditions under which classical brand equity theory retains full explanatory validity and those beyond which brand evaluation becomes distributed across human and algorithmic evaluative systems, providing a new theoretical architecture for understanding how brand value is generated, evaluated, and converted into competitive outcomes in markets characterized by high algorithmic mediation.

detail.title: The Anatomy of Transmission: Pass-Through of Market Rates to Bank Deposit Rates in the Euro Area

publicationDetails.detailsText: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 865
publicationDetails.journalName: De Nederlandsche Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the pass-through of market rates to bank deposit rates in the euro area, using bank-level data from July 2007 to March 2025. We employ local projections and an errorcorrection model to analyze the dynamics of pass-through over time, across interest rate regimes, and among countries, as well as explore its potential drivers. The results show that
pass-through is significant but uneven. It is stronger for term and corporate deposits than for demand and household deposits. The effectiveness of pass-through diminishes in a lowinterest- rate environment and varies across countries. Structural features of the banking sector and bank balance sheet characteristics also shape transmission. Specifically, banks operating in more concentrated markets exhibit lower pass-through. In addition, banks with larger liquidity buffers, stronger capitalization, and greater reliance on deposit funding adjust deposit rates less. Lastly, higher customer switching frequency and higher payment account fees are associated with stronger pass-through for household demand deposits.

title: Assessing the Effects of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Higher Education Outcomes: Evidence from Ethiopian Public Universities

detail.title: Assessing the Effects of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Higher Education Outcomes: Evidence from Ethiopian Public Universities
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education by enhancing teaching, learning, research, and administrative processes. Technologies such as machine learning, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI provide significant opportunities to improve educational quality, relevance, and accessibility while addressing the demands of the digital era. Despite these advancements, empirical evidence on the impact of AI adoption in higher education remains limited in developing countries, particularly Ethiopia. This study examined the effect of AI adoption on higher education outcomes in Ethiopian public universities, focusing on relevance, quality, and accessibility. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from academic and administrative staff using a structured questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and multiple regression analysis were used to analyze the data. The findings reveal that AI adoption is widely perceived as enhancing curriculum modernization, student engagement, personalized learning, research productivity, and educational inclusiveness. Regression results indicate that AI adoption has a positive and statistically significant effect on the relevance of higher education (β = 0.220, p < 0.001) and accessibility (β = 0.151, p = 0.016). Although AI also demonstrated a positive effect on educational quality (β = 0.113), the relationship was only marginally significant (p = 0.074). Overall, the findings suggest that AI adoption has considerable potential to strengthen higher education outcomes, particularly by improving relevance and accessibility. The study recommends increased investment in digital infrastructure, institutional capacity building, faculty development, and supportive policy frameworks to accelerate the effective integration of AI across Ethiopian public universities.

detail.title: A Decade of Tracking Financial Literacy in America. Findings from the 2026 TIAA Institute–GFLEC Personal Finance Index

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The 2026 P-Fin Index marks a decade of tracking financial literacy among U.S. adults, and the milestone brings sobering news. Americans correctly answered only 47% of the index's 28 questions on average, a statistically significant decline from the prior year and the lowest result in the survey's 10-year history. The share of adults with very low financial literacy has grown steadily from 20% in 2017 to 25% in 2026, with the most pronounced gaps among Gen Z, who correctly answered only 38% of questions on average. Financial literacy has declined significantly in five of the eight functional knowledge areas covered by the index: consuming, borrowing, earning, insuring, and comprehending risk indicating that the decline is broad-based, not concentrated in a single topic. Gender gaps persist across nearly all functional areas, with women scoring 6 percentage points lower than men overall. To mark the survey's 10-year anniversary, the researchers developed and publicly released the P-Fin 8 Index, an abbreviated eight-question measure that closely tracks the full index and is now available for use by researchers and practitioners.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Law and Political Economy, No. 5(3)
publicationDetails.journalName: Journal of Law & Political Economy

detail.abstract: This article clarifies standards for evaluating whether a firm's unilateral labor market conduct (wage suppression) violates antitrust law. It begins by analyzing suppression of collective bargaining (union busting) as conduct that can violate Section 2 of the Sherman Act. This article is the first to argue that wage suppression can violate Section 2 if the conduct (1) harms the competitive process within a labor market and increases monopsony, (2) tends to exclude law-abiding rivals from product or service markets, or (3) forecloses any adjacent market. Conduct that satisfies any of these three standards can be restrained with antitrust law. The antitrust standards presented are applicable to any kind of unilateral labor market conduct, including worker misclassification, wage theft, vertical restraints, restrictive covenants, employer-driven debt, or child labor.

detail.title: Communication Failure: The Hidden Face of The Tragedy of the Commons

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies communication failure regarding risks in the commons. It argues that strategic issues might explain why years of scientific reporting regarding future risks have failed to trigger sufficient climate awareness. We consider a game of contribution to a public bad, where there is uncertainty regarding the damage generated by externalities. Prior to the game, agents receive non-certifiable information regarding the damage from an informed utilitarian expert. We show that in large-scale public good problems information transmission usually fails. We compare this result with the cases of Rawlsian and anti-Rawlsian experts and discuss the implication for climate expert panels. We also investigate the influence of the value of information in our result, which provides us with some insight on the part played by deontology on scientific communication.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of mayors' gender in shaping public procurement at the local level. Using a Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) and unique datasets on Italian procurement records, firm-level data, and political information spanning 2013-2019, we explore whether procurement contracts published under female mayors exhibit different outcomes compared to those under male mayors in close elections. The results indicate modest differences in procurement practices between female and male mayors: female mayors rely less on negotiated contracts and more on direct awards. Female leadership is also associated with fewer renegotiations and a (surprisingly) lower likelihood of appointing female procurement officers, while no differences emerge in winner characteristics or other post-award outcomes. ✯ The authors acknowledge financial support from the Italian Ministry of Education Grant no. 2017Y5PJ43 001 PRIN 2017. We thank Clarissa Lotti and Silvia Vannutelli for insightful comments and discussions.

No external party influenced the study design, analysis, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only publicly available, anonymized market data (MEXC Spot BTC/USDT) and involves no human participants, patients, or personal data; ethics approval is therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All compute was self-funded on the author's own consumer hardware.

detail.abstract: We ask whether large language models (LLMs), reading a compressed order-book/trade-flow snapshot, produce signals that incrementally predict short-horizon crypto market dynamicsand, in particular, whether disagreement between heterogeneous base models predicts forward realized volatility (RV). We pre-register the hypotheses, the metric, the materiality thresholds, and the kill gates before computing any result, and we enforce a firewall that gates expensive live data collection behind cheap offline pilots. On real MEXC Spot BTC/USDT data (a 50,277snapshot corpus collected over two live runs), we report a four-way falsification: neither (i) single-model directional bias, (ii) single-model conviction magnitude, (iii) single-model sampling dispersion, nor (iv) inter-model disagreement clears its pre-registered incremental bar at 5/15/30minute horizons. The headline hypothesis-inter-model disagreement → forward RV-is killed decisively and triple-robustly at n ≈ 21,905 (15-minute partial Spearman +0.010, MBB 95% CI [-0.006, +0.027], well inside ±0.05). The mechanism is a positive, publishable finding in its own right: heterogeneous base models reading the same compressed snapshot converge on directional bias (in-sample rank agreement ≈ 0.49; best available cross-lineage decorrelation only |ρ| = 0.56), so the disagreement signal has little headroom and what little exists is orthogonal to volatility. The contribution is methodological: a pre-registered, provenance-fingerprinted, compute-controlled evaluation pipeline that distinguishes signal from the volatility-clustering confound (which inflates the marginal correlations roughly threefold), in a literature where over-claiming P&L backtests are the norm.

title: Methodologies for Calibrating and Backtesting Probability of Default Using Quarterly Default Rates in Line with Basel Guidelines
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Methodologies for Calibrating and Backtesting Probability of Default Using Quarterly Default Rates in Line with Basel Guidelines
detail.abstract:
Probability of Default (PD) estimation is a crucial component of credit risk modeling, particularly for regulatory compliance under Basel guidelines (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2019). The calibration and backtesting of PDs are essential to ensure accuracy, stability, and regulatory soundness; specifically, the estimation of PD can be mathematically represented by the equation in the paper. This paper explores methodologies for PD calibration using quarterly default rates, focusing on statistical, Bayesian, and machine learning approaches; Bayesian estimation, for instance, employs prior distributions leading to posterior updates through Bayes theorem. It also examines backtesting techniques to validate PD estimates, including binomial tests, which assess the null hypothesis that the observed default rate aligns with the estimated PD, traffic light approaches for assessing thresholds, and time-series analysis to evaluate predictability over time (Koyluoglu et al., 2021). 

The study highlights the challenges associated with low-default portfolios (LDPs) which require specialized statistical techniques such as bootstrapping to enhance estimation reliability, and presents best practices for regulatory alignment, emphasizing the importance of maintaining model accuracy in a constantly evolving economic landscape. Furthermore, these methodologies are situated within a broader discussion of methodological rigor in empirical research, reflecting the iterative revision process necessary for scholarly communication and the integration of evidence-based argumentation across related topics. Keywords: Analytical Research Writing, Academic Writing, Research Paper Structure, Thesis Development, Evidence-Based Argumentation, Methodological Rigor, Critical Analysis, Scholarly Communication, Literature Review Integration, Argument Structuring, Peer Review Process, Theoretical Frameworks, Writing Clarity and Coherence, Iterative Revision Process, Academic Discourse.

title: Anomalies, Data Snooping, and Post-Publication Decay: Evidence from the Super Bowl Predictor
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Anomalies, Data Snooping, and Post-Publication Decay: Evidence from the Super Bowl Predictor
detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to revisit the effectiveness of the Super Bowl Stock Market Predictor (SBSMP) hypothesis, which suggests that the yearly S&P 500 return rates are dependent on whether the Super Bowl champion belongs to the NFC (National Football Conference) or the AFC (American Football Conference). Using accuracy decomposition analysis, t-tests, OLS regression, and the Bonferroni correction over a period ranging from 1967 to 2025, it was found that the accuracy of the SBSMP dropped from 66.7% over the 1967-1999 period to 46.7% during 2000-2014 and a record low of 18.2% over 2015-2025. In addition, a two-sample t-test yielded results that the average return rate of NFC champions (+13.50%) and AFC champions (+10.76%) is not significantly different at t = 0.6374 with a p-value of 0.5265. The NFC dummy variable was not significant in all models with a Bonferroni-corrected p-value of 1.0000. A bootstrap simulation shows that the probability of observing the 91% success rate by chance was 0.0001, which confirms the original KK figure was statistically unusual but did not persist out of sample. Meanwhile, a Chow test for a structural break indicates a significant change in the regression relationship between the conference and returns per year at the 2000 threshold. All of these findings support the theory of post-publication decay.

title: Freight-Market Regimes and Risk-Aware Portfolio Allocation in Shipping Equities

detail.title: Freight-Market Regimes and Risk-Aware Portfolio Allocation in Shipping Equities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the research reported in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether observable freight-market regimes enhance dynamic allocation in listed shipping equities through state-dependent return and covariance estimation. Freight regimes are constructed from Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) momentum, realized volatility, drawdown, correlation stress, and a seasonal autoregressive freight-outlook signal. The resulting expansion, contraction, and turbulence states are used to estimate regime-specific return vectors and covariance matrices, which are embedded in a constrained finite-horizon Hamilton-Bellman portfolio problem solved using a finite-volume method. The empirical design is fully walk-forward: regime thresholds, return-risk estimates, and portfolio weights are updated using only information available before each rebalancing date. The results indicate that the regime conditioned HJB-FVM strategy delivers a higher Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown relative to equal weighting and outperforms a static HJB benchmark. Nevertheless, equal weighting generates slightly higher terminal wealth and annualized return. The evidence supports a cautious interpretation: freight-market regimes appear to be more useful for controlling downside risk in shipping-equity portfolios than for maximizing raw cumulative returns.

title: Verification for the Buyer, Not the Seller: A Deployed Construction-Quote Gate

detail.title: Verification for the Buyer, Not the Seller: A Deployed Construction-Quote Gate

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the developer and operator of the live construction-cost service in which the verification gate described in this paper is deployed. No other financial or personal relationships influenced the study. The system is operated on a commercial basis; this paper reports its design and observed behavior and makes no efficacy or performance claims beyond the demonstrations described.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects, and did not require ethics approval. The demonstrations use the author's own deployed system.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The current generation of AI tools for construction cost is built, almost without exception, to help the contractor quote faster, protect margin, and suggest upsells; it puts the informational advantage on the seller's side of a market where the buyer already cannot tell whether a quote is fair. This paper reports a tool built for the other side. Residential construction is a credence good, a purchase whose fair price the buyer cannot verify even after the work is done, and the economics of such markets holds that giving the buyer a means of verification would close the asymmetry. Yet when a large laboratory experiment (Dulleck, Kerschbamer, and Sutter, 2011) granted buyers verifiability, it changed market efficiency at best slightly, leaving a twenty-year puzzle. A feature of that work is easy to miss and central here: verifiability was handed to the buyer as a rule of the experiment, whereas in a real market no buyer has any instrument with which to verify a construction quote at all, and none has been deployed and studied. That tool is a verification gate, running in a live construction-cost service, that admits buyer-contributed quotations to a shared comparison board while preventing a malicious or mistaken contribution from corrupting it. The gate treats the model that reads a contribution as untrusted, allowing it only to propose structured fields with verbatim source spans and no capability to admit, write, or act; it verifies each field against the contribution's own text, re-derives reliability from agreement across repeated extractions rather than from the model's confidence, and decides by a deterministic, content-hashed function. Because the deciding component cannot act on an instruction, an instruction embedded in a contribution has no path to the decision, which we show at runtime as an invariance: the decision is unchanged whether the instruction is present or absent. The gate's components, untrusted proposal, source-grounded verification, deterministic re-verification, capability denial, and cryptographic auditability, are drawn from existing work and none is claimed as novel. The contribution is the position and the setting: to our knowledge the first deployed, buyer-side, verification-only gate in this credence-good market, offered as a field artifact for a verifiability question the discipline has examined only in the laboratory, and demonstrated on a live deployment through a controlled injection pair, a fabricated-field refusal, a fail-closed response to extractor failure, and reproducible decisions.

title: A Process of "Trial and Error": How the EU Courts Affect the Council's Sanctions Designation Practice
affiliations: Ghent University and University of Luxembourg

detail.title: A Process of "Trial and Error": How the EU Courts Affect the Council's Sanctions Designation Practice
detail.abstract: The Council of the European Union (EU) enjoys a broad margin of appreciation when adopting, amending and renewing restrictive measures targeting natural and legal persons. Yet this discretion is not without limits. To balance the specificities of the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) with the need for effective judicial protection, the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) has developed a twofold approach: a deferential review of designation criteria paired with a more intensive, evidence-based review of individual listing decisions. This article examines how that approach has shaped the Council's listing practice, focusing on the evolution of designation criteria for both primary and secondary targets and the growing diversification of listing grounds aimed at countering sanctions circumvention and Russian hybrid threats. The analysis shows that the adoption and renewal of restrictive measures is a process of continuous "trial and error", driven by the interaction between the EU courts and the Council. This dynamic has produced paradoxical consequences. In particular, broader and more flexible designation criteria introduced in response to judicial scrutiny may increase the Council's evidentiary burden, creating new opportunities for listed persons to challenge their designation. This ongoing cycle raises broader questions about the legitimacy and effectiveness of the EU's sanctions policy.

title: Effects of Incentivizing Novelty vs. Usefulness and Idea Sharing Policies on Idea Sharing and Subsequent Collaboration
affiliations: , Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management and

detail.title: Effects of Incentivizing Novelty vs. Usefulness and Idea Sharing Policies on Idea Sharing and Subsequent Collaboration
detail.abstract: We examine how creativity incentives emphasizing novelty versus usefulness and sharing policies jointly affect employees’ willingness to share ideas and their subsequent collaboration. We predict that novelty incentives heighten evaluation apprehension relative to usefulness incentives because novelty invites greater comparison across ideas, reducing voluntary sharing. We further predict that mandating a minimum level of sharing can offset this effect by normalizing sharing. In our main experiment, participants each generate three slogans under novelty or usefulness incentives and either choose how many slogans to share or are required to share at least one. Novelty incentives reduce idea sharing when it is fully voluntary, but the minimum sharing requirement mitigates this effect by increasing both total sharing and sharing beyond the required minimum. We also find that under novelty incentives, participants collaborate more on a subsequent group task when sharing is voluntary than when it is mandatory. A supplemental experiment suggests that voluntary sharing increases perceptions of a collaborative culture, whereas higher sharing levels produced by mandates can heighten perceived competition. Together, our findings identify evaluation apprehension as a key barrier to idea sharing under novelty incentives and highlight an important tradeoff in designing idea sharing policies.

title: Nonbanks, Deposit Franchises, and Monetary Policy Transmission
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank - Research Centre

detail.title: Nonbanks, Deposit Franchises, and Monetary Policy Transmission
detail.abstract: Funding structure, not depository status, governs monetary policy transmission to U.S. mortgage borrowers. Within county-year cells spanning 23.5 million HMDA loans, mortgage companies amplify rate-spread responses by 1.30 percentage points per percentage-point surprise relative to banks; credit unions dampen them by 0.92 points. Credit unions are statistically indistinguishable from low-deposit-beta banks: the insured deposit franchise, not charter or supervision, is the primitive. A spatial competition model rationalizes the hierarchy, predicting endogenous reallocation, self-correcting transmission, and concentration-dependent attenuation, each empirically supported. Composition shifts added 0.20 points to pass-through by the 2021 peak, making transmission state-dependent. Binary nonbank classications obscure this heterogeneity.

title: The Impact Of Agricultural Supply Chain Disruptions On Headline Inflation In Malawi

detail.title: The Impact Of Agricultural Supply Chain Disruptions On Headline Inflation In Malawi

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the conduct or reporting of this research. No external parties influenced the research design, data collection, analysis, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data from national and international institutions including the Reserve Bank of Malawi, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, NASA, Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority, and the United States Department of Agriculture. No human participants were involved and no ethics approval was required.

detail.abstract: Inflation in Malawi is not an abstract statistic. It is the transport fare that doubled before wages moved, the fuel queue that delays inputs from reaching farms, and the exchange rate movement that raises landing costs before any policy response arrives. At the centre of these dynamics sits agriculture, a sector generating over 80% of export earnings, determining foreign exchange availability, shaping the economy's capacity to import fuel and fertiliser, and ultimately governing the conditions under which goods move from farms to markets to households. This study investigates the impact of agricultural supply chain disruptions on headline inflation in Malawi using annual time-series data from 1970 to 2024. A Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) captures dynamic relationships between headline inflation, climatic shocks proxied by annual rainfall, fertiliser prices, fuel prices, and exchange rate movements. Johansen cointegration tests confirm stable long-run equilibrium relationships among variables integrated of order one. Exchange rate depreciation emerges as the dominant long-run driver of inflation, inseparable from agricultural performance given the sector's control over export earnings and forex generation. Fuel price shocks transmit strongly through transport and distribution costs across the supply chain. Climatic shocks influence inflation through production cycles with a lag consistent with harvest timing. Contrary to standard costpush assumptions, fertiliser prices exert no statistically significant effect on headline inflation, a finding explained by the cushioning role of government subsidy programmes and household remittances that insulate smallholder farmers from global input price movements. The error correction coefficient of-0.48 indicates rapid adjustment toward long-run equilibrium. Controlling inflation in Malawi requires more than monetary tightening and praying for good rains; it requires strengthening agricultural supply chains, improving energy logistics, and building structural resilience to shocks that cascade through the entire economy.

title: Private Tax Incentives and Public Borrowing Costs: Evidence from Opportunity Zones
affiliations: ,  and University of Pittsburgh - Finance Group

detail.title: Private Tax Incentives and Public Borrowing Costs: Evidence from Opportunity Zones
detail.abstract: We examine whether Opportunity Zones, a federal place-based program that provides capital-gains tax incentives for private investment in designated low-income communities, affect local governments' cost of capital. Although OZs subsidize private investors rather than municipal issuers, counties with higher OZ exposure experience lower secondary-market municipal bond yields after the program's introduction. The effect is strongest for general obligation bonds and is concentrated in counties with lower pretreatment debt burdens and stronger credit profiles, consistent with investors capitalizing OZ exposure when expected private-development gains are more credible and more pledgeable to municipal bondholders. Primary-market evidence shows similar patterns in new borrowing terms. County-level fiscal, construction, housing, and industry outcomes provide mechanistic evidence that the bond-market response is accompanied by changes in local fundamentals relevant for municipal credit risk. Overall, the findings show that private-capital place-based tax incentives can affect public borrowing costs even when local governments are not the direct recipients of the subsidy.

detail.title: Why Climate Policies Fail to Prevent Tipping Points
detail.abstract: Climate policies have failed to prevent ecological tipping points despite three decades of international commitments and over 1,500 policy interventions across 41 countries. Yet existing evaluation frameworks assess policy success solely through emissions reductions, leaving unanswered the critical question of whether any policy instrument has meaningfully reduced the probability of crossing irreversible ecological thresholds. Here, we develop a theoretical model of optimal climate policy design under tipping risk, integrating dynamic optimisation with decision theory to formalise how a policymaker balances short-term political payoffs against the risk of irreversible ecological collapse. We demonstrate that policies designed for emissions reduction are structurally misaligned with tipping point prevention, and that rational policymakers-discounting the future heavily-will knowingly accept this misalignment. This leads to a fundamental tension between politically optimal policy and ecologically safe policy. Our framework identifies the narrow conditions under which climate instruments can function as effective tipping point governance tools, offering a theoretical foundation for the next generation of climate policy design.

title:
The Evidence Imperative: Knowing Every Learner as the Foundation of Adaptive Education.
 A White Paper on UK's Explore Learning's Evidence-Based Approach to AI and Technology Adoption in Childhood Education
affiliations: UWE Bristol, Department of Computer Science

detail.title:
The Evidence Imperative: Knowing Every Learner as the Foundation of Adaptive Education.
 A White Paper on UK's Explore Learning's Evidence-Based Approach to AI and Technology Adoption in Childhood Education
detail.abstract:
Education technology is expanding fast: the global market is projected at USD 348 billion by 2030 and the UK sector at USD 31.15 billion, growth driven largely by AI, machine learning and generative tools such as large language models. That growth carries both promise and risk. Meta-analytic evidence shows AI interventions can lift academic performance substantially (effect size d = 0.92), yet the same tools raise concerns for higher-order cognition: over-reliance is linked to shallower critical thinking and to cognitive fixation that weakens creative confidence.

This paradox, stronger measurable outcomes alongside a possible erosion of deeper thinking, calls for a different approach to AI in education: evidence over hype, knowing the learner over algorithmic convenience, and human guidance over technological displacement.

Explore Learning's core thesis is that genuine personalisation is impossible without rigorous, ongoing assessment of each child's zone of proximal development, learning rate and mastery trajectory. Technology should serve that understanding, not replace it. The white paper sets out an evidence-based framework in which continuous learner understanding is the precondition for adaptive learning, and it is critical of EdTech that promises personalisation without the evidential infrastructure to deliver it.

title: Civil Macroeconomics
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics, University of Catania, University of Pavia, LUMSA University and University of Perugia - Department of Economics

detail.title: Civil Macroeconomics
detail.abstract: The dominant macroeconomic framework rests mainly on two intertwined assumptions: (i) the reduction of macroeconomic dynamics to the optimizing behavior of a representative agent; and (ii) the substantial neutrality of monetary and fiscal policies, conceived essentially as tools aimed at stabilizing prices, output gap, and public finances indexes without adequate consideration for their significant effects on the ethical, relational, structural, and institutional features of the economic systems. We contend that this framework is inherently unable to account for the complex relational interactions among heterogeneous economic agents and feebacks between key quantitative macroeconomic phenomena, on the one side, and emerging factors such as cooperation, social trust, institutional legitimacy, resilience to systemic shocks, and long-term sustainable wellbeing, on the other. We advance a new foundation for macroeconomics grounded in the recognition of the biodiverse and relational nature of economic reality. Individuals, as persons with their own uniqueness, have also other-regarding preferences and are capable of "relational intelligence". Firms and intermediate institutions operate with plural objectives (overall impact and not just profits); and macroeconomic outcomes emerge from complex interaction processes between heterogeneous agents with a key role for economic policy decisions and the formation of prevailing expectations in condition of systemic uncertainty. On this basis, we argue that macroeconomic policies cannot be neutral. Monetary and government authorities inevitably take sides by either reinforcing extractive and short-term equilibria or actively promoting generativity, participation, subsidiarity, relational goods, and life flourishing. We therefore propose a civil macroeconomic framework in which central banking, government policy (including, in addition to fiscal policy, also industrial and innovation policies and regulation decisions), public debt management and trade and exchange rate policies are explicitly purpose-driven, oriented toward the structural expansion of capabilities and the improvement of sustainable and inclusive wellbeing rather than the sole stabilization of conventional aggregates. Illustrative policy implications include socially and environmentally targeted monetary interventions, generativity-oriented fiscal incentives and regulations, and debt strategies preserving market trust through policy makers' cooperation and coordination aligned with intergenerational justice and ecological and social sustainability. In the international domain, the framework supports open trade and exchange-rate regimes only insofar as they are institutionally designed to prevent races to the bottom in labour, health, and environmental standards, combining openness with minimum global floors, supply-chain responsibility, and macroeconomic coordination to preserve trust, legitimacy, and long-term wellbeing. By reframing macroeconomics as a science of emergent collective dynamics rather than a mere optimization of an individual choice, the paper contributes to ongoing debates on the foundations of macroeconomic theory and offers a normative and analytical basis for a civil-oriented redesign of macroeconomic policy.

title: Local Versus Accumulated Angle in Hyperbolic Flows: Implications for the Quantum Riemann Analogue
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Local Versus Accumulated Angle in Hyperbolic Flows: Implications for the Quantum Riemann Analogue
detail.abstract: The Riemann zeta function ζ(s) has inspired a celebrated analogy in quantum chaos: for a quantum system whose classical limit is fully chaotic, the zeros of the spectral determinant are conjectured to lie on a straight line Im(E) = λ/2, where λ is the classical Lyapunov exponent. This is the quantum analogue of the Riemann hypothesis. This paper investigates a geometric necessary condition for this conjecture: constancy of the Lyapunov exponent, equivalently dβ/dt = λ.

title: Joint Predictions and Counterfactuals under Symmetric Latent Information

detail.title: Joint Predictions and Counterfactuals under Symmetric Latent Information
detail.abstract: This paper studies joint prediction and counterfactual analysis for an observed game and a counterfactual game when the information structure is latent to the analyst but common across the two. The observed and counterfactual games are assumed to belong to a maintained symmetric class: payoffs are symmetric, private types are exchangeable, and additional signals satisfy a symmetric conditional-independence restriction. I construct a linked game that encodes fixed information across the two games. SBCE of the linked base game yields an exact characterization of the joint outcome distributions induced by symmetric Bayes Nash equilibrium as the common admissible information structure ranges over the class. The resulting fixed-information counterfactual prediction set is contained in the unrestricted BCE counterfactual prediction set of the same linked base game. In the two-firm entry environment of Bergemann et al. (2022), this containment is strict: for positive payoff shifters z in (0,1), the SBCE producer-surplus prediction set is the singleton equal to 2, whereas unrestricted BCE of the linked base game allows producer surplus to move both above and below 2. Thus these primitive restrictions can have counterfactual content beyond the fixed-information requirement itself.

title: Consuming Out of Trade Wars: Evidence from Chinese Households
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE), Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) - School of International Business and University of International Business and Economics

detail.title: Consuming Out of Trade Wars: Evidence from Chinese Households
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the US-China tariff war on Chinese household consumption. Exploiting pre-war variation in trading partners and product compositions across Chinese cities, we construct city-level measures of export exposure to US tariffs and import exposure to Chinese retaliatory tariffs. Using a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach, we unexpectedly find that Chinese retaliatory tariffs persistently harm household consumption, whereas US tariffs show no such effect. While we find no evidence supporting the conventional consumer price channel, our results suggest that depressed household income and reduced propensity to consume are the driving forces, with the latter being particularly important in the long run. We further disentangle import tariff exposure into that from consumption goods versus intermediate goods, finding that the latter drives the results, suggesting that retaliatory tariffs can inadvertently harm domestic welfare through supply chain linkages. Finally, we explore distributional effects across households and geographic spillovers across regions.

detail.abstract: Agricultural export restrictions are widely used to stabilise domestic markets, contain food inflation, and safeguard food security. However, relatively little evidence exists on the market conditions associated with export restriction episodes across different commodities. This paper examines agricultural export restriction episodes in India for six major commodities-rice, wheat, maize, onion, cotton, and sugar-using monthly data from April 2007 to March 2025. Pearson correlation analysis is used as an exploratory descriptive tool for the relationship between export restrictions and eight variables representing domestic market conditions, international market signals, macroeconomic influences and environmental factors. The results reveal substantial variation across commodities. Rice and onion restriction episodes are strongly associated with domestic price pressures (ρ = 0.619 and 0.265, respectively) and international prices (ρ = 0.610 and 0.366), broadly consistent with the conventional price-stabilisation rationale. In contrast, wheat restrictions are most closely associated with exchange rate movements (ρ = 0.847) and production conditions (ρ = 0.816), while domestic prices exhibit virtually no relationship with restriction episodes. Maize exhibits a contrasting pattern where restrictions are negatively associated with prices and production. Cotton restrictions are most strongly correlated with production dynamics (ρ = 0.664), whereas sugar presents a multidimensional pattern involving domestic demand (ρ = 0.717), exchange rates (ρ = 0.632), domestic production and prices. The findings overall suggest that episodes of export restriction are associated with commodity-specific market environments rather than a common set of market conditions in India. The results suggest the need for more differentiated and evidence-based approaches to agricultural trade policy.

title: The Federal Reserve as the World's Unofficial Central Bank
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: The Federal Reserve as the World's Unofficial Central Bank

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in the Cornell Law Review (August 2026)

detail.abstract:
The Federal Reserve (Fed) has quietly become the world’s de facto central bank. Acting as the global lender of last resort, it has backstopped the global economy through central bank swap lines—bilateral agreements with foreign central banks—that supplied more than half a trillion dollars during the Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19. Five of those agreements now function as standing, uncapped guarantees of dollar liquidity.

This Article explains how and why the Fed came to occupy this role. Drawing on extensive archival evidence, it argues that the Fed’s global authority emerged through a century-long, path-dependent process in which repeated crises reallocated authority away from the political branches and international organizations and to the central bank. It decouples the Fed’s institutional rise from the dollar’s structural dominance, tracing the Fed's global rise instead to its comparative institutional advantages—money creation, legal latitude, and central bank coordination—that made its interventions easier to deploy and harder to displace.

In this new light, the Fed’s global role is both a product and a driver of hegemonic succession—from sterling to dollar, and perhaps now toward renminbi. An original dataset shows that while the Fed remains the central node in a system of proliferating liquidity agreements that structure “weaponized interdependence,” rival networks—notably China’s—are emerging as nascent monetary circuits atop the global dollar order.

title: The Missing Jury: Fact, Law, and Who Actually Decides Trademark Confusion

detail.title: The Missing Jury: Fact, Law, and Who Actually Decides Trademark Confusion
detail.abstract: On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in RiseandShine Corp. v. PepsiCo to decide whether a trademark’s strength is a question of fact, typically for a jury, or a question of law for a judge. This Essay measures the assumption beneath the question: that a jury is available to receive it. Across 10,977 federal likelihood-of-confusion opinions, judges made 97.96% of merits confusion determinations; juries made 2.04%. The strength factor specifically was graded at a jury trial 2.04% of the time it was graded at all, a different cohort landing on the same rounded share. Docket-level data confirm the picture from outside the opinions: in fiscal 2025, just twenty-seven trademark cases in the entire federal system reached a jury. Four empirical studies across twenty years have now converged on this result, each at larger scale and finer resolution. This Essay is neutral on the question presented and specific about the terrain: whichever decision-maker wins the label, the question will operate almost entirely at summary judgment, in the rare contested case, on a paper record. In operation, either answer regulates a judge, and the choice is between standards of judicial self-restraint, inside a multifactor test whose accumulated evidence now counsels simplification.

title: A Transparent, Set-Identified Framework for Cross-Era NBA Player Ranking: Possession-Clock Deflation, Skill-Environment Attribution, and Multi-Layer Validation

detail.title: A Transparent, Set-Identified Framework for Cross-Era NBA Player Ranking: Possession-Clock Deflation, Skill-Environment Attribution, and Multi-Layer Validation
detail.abstract: Cross-era comparison of athletes is usually treated as opinion because nominal box-score output is not comparable across leagues whose scoring environment, pace, and rules differ by tens of percent. We address it with an explicit, axiomatic measurement framework -- borrowing the asset-pricing metaphor of deflating nominal returns and separating skill from market exposure, not its no-arbitrage machinery -- under which a few stated value axioms characterize a specific valuation functional, leaving only a transparent, validation-identified weight set. Five results form the spine: a deflation operator that re-expresses production on the possession clock and deflates by league efficiency, with inputs downloaded from public tables; an attribution theorem making individual skill the orthogonal projection off the teammate/environment subspace, with a near-collinear media regressor (VIF = 6.29) down-weighted for that reason; a credit theorem proving the load-proportional championship share is the exact Shapley value of an additive game; a representation theorem that derives, rather than posits, the linear score from ordinal axioms; and an identification theorem casting calibration as set-identification, so a ranking conclusion is objective-given-the-axioms iff its margin is sign-invariant on the identified set, with a breakdown distance grading robustness. The paper's contribution is the framework, not any individual placement. On sixteen players over fully recomputable public data the resulting ranking is led by Jordan and is parameter-invariant on 98.2% of the identified set, surviving five-cutoff forward tests, a 6075-point grid, Monte Carlo (P = 97.8%), a 4500-specification multiverse, permutation diagnostics (p = 0.009), and breakdown analysis; we use the placements that diverge most from media consensus (Olajuwon 5th, James 11th, Bird 12th) as case studies of how the value function operates. We do not claim to settle the ranking in any absolute sense; the contribution is an explicit, reproducible, stress-tested value function under which, and within whose validation-identified weight set, several conclusions are highly robust, a posture we call conditional objectivity.

title: Collateral Damage or Collateral Advantage? Crypto Entry into the Financial Mainstream

detail.abstract:
The Federal Reserve’s decision in August 2025 to fold its Novel Activities Supervision Program into standard banking oversight marks a turning point in the treatment of digital assets in the United States. What was once dismissed as speculation is now edging toward mainstream acceptance within existing legal and regulatory frameworks.
In this article, the author argues that crypto assets, properly governed by Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code, Basel capital and liquidity standards, and prudential supervisory practices, are increasingly poised to serve as eligible collateral in U.S. financial markets. The analysis examines the evolution of regulatory guidance, the mechanics of collateral and repo markets, the lessons of high-profile failures such as Terra, Celsius, and FTX, and the systemic risk implications of haircut policy and contagion. It situates these debates within broader macroeconomic and geopolitical
contexts, contending that assimilation, rather than segregation, offers the most resilient path forward.

title: A Local-Volatility Theory of Prediction Markets: Absorbed Martingales on the Simplex and an Identification Law for Transient Mispricing

detail.title: A Local-Volatility Theory of Prediction Markets: Absorbed Martingales on the Simplex and an Identification Law for Transient Mispricing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: A prediction-market contract pays a fixed amount contingent on an event; under no-arbitrage its price is a bounded martingale absorbed at the outcome vertices at a known horizon, so the Black-Scholes geometric-Brownian framework does not transfer. We make two central theoretical contributions and confront them with high-frequency contract data. First, we develop a general local-volatility theory for absorbed event-market martingales: we characterize the admissible class of efficient-price dynamics by a boundary-degeneracy condition, give the general information-clock volatility Sigma_t = phi(Phi^{-1}(p)) sqrt(nu_t/R_t), and show that the normal-threshold Brownian kernel is the maximum-entropy canonical member. A simplex-structure theorem unifies binary, three-outcome, and n-outcome contracts, with closed-form Skellam jump pricing of football markets as a worked instance. Second, we prove an identification law for transient mispricing: for any stationary transitory component, lag-one return autocorrelation decays as O(1/Delta) in the sampling interval, so above the mispricing time scale the sampled price is second-moment indistinguishable from the efficient martingale. A signature lemma shows that the shape of the autocorrelation-versus-frequency curve separates bid-ask-bounce microstructure noise from genuine overreaction, and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck instance gives a closed-form observability law. Empirically, on 66 Polymarket and 50 Kalshi 2026 World-Cup matches, covering 2.8 million Kalshi trades, the data are consistent with the kernel and show bounce-corrected autocorrelation that is significantly negative below about 10 seconds and positive beyond about 30 seconds. Robustness checks show that the short-horizon reversion survives a same-aggressor-side bounce control and strengthens once goal-jump windows are excluded, while a real bid/ask spread backtest confirms that the reversion is genuine but not exploitable by liquidity taking; whether it is harvestable by liquidity provision is left open.

title: Uzbekistan's Economic Recovery After COVID-19: An Analysis of Key Macroeconomic Indicators (2019–2024)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Uzbekistan's Economic Recovery After COVID-19: An Analysis of Key Macroeconomic Indicators (2019–2024)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic trajectory of Uzbekistan in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, analyzing key macroeconomic indicators including GDP growth, unemployment, inflation, and remittance flows during the period 2019–2024. Drawing on data from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the Asian Development Bank, this study documents how Uzbekistan's economy — despite experiencing a sharp slowdown in 2020 — demonstrated notable resilience, recovering to pre-crisis growth levels by 2021. The analysis highlights the critical role of government fiscal stimulus, monetary policy adjustments, and remittance inflows in sustaining household consumption during the crisis period. However, the paper also identifies persistent structural vulnerabilities, including high dependence on remittances from Russia, elevated inflation, and labor market fragility. The findings suggest that while Uzbekistan's short-term recovery has been relatively successful, long-term sustainable growth will require deeper structural reforms, private sector development, and reduced external dependency.

title: Data Guilds, Synthetic Labor Tax, and Recursive Legitimacy: Designing Fiscal and Institutional Mechanisms for an AI Social Contract
